Retrieved text and figure-based context are then provided to an open-weight large language model, which generates the final responses grounded in the retrieved evidence.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent RAG framework with vision-language capabilities for knowledge management in transportation agencies, addressing fragmented expertise and information retrieval challenges.
AI.motivation: Traditional knowledge management approaches in state transportation agencies (static documentation, classroom instruction, informal mentorship) lead to fragmented knowledge transfer, inefficiencies, and loss of expertise as senior engineers retire. The enormous volume of technical materials makes it difficult for engineers to quickly locate relevant information for field problems or training tasks, hindering timely decision-making and creating steep learning curves for new personnel.
AI.method: Proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework with multi-agent architecture. System integrates structured document retrieval with real-time, context-aware response generation using LLM. Employs multiple specialized agents for retrieval, answer generation, evaluation, and query refinement for iterative improvement and quality control. Incorporates open-weight vision-language model to convert technical figures into semantic textual representations, enabling figure-based knowledge indexing and retrieval alongside text. Retrieved text and figure-based context are provided to an open-weight LLM for evidence-grounded response generation.
AI.result: The paper proposes a framework but does not present experimental results in the abstract. The system design integrates multiple components: multi-agent RAG architecture, vision-language model for figure processing, and open-weight LLM for response generation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent RAG framework with vision-language capabilities addresses critical knowledge management challenges in transportation agencies by enabling efficient retrieval of both textual and visual information, supporting evidence-based decision making, and facilitating knowledge transfer through an iterative, quality-controlled system architecture.

title: A Rubric-Supervised Critic from Sparse Real-World Outcomes
summary: Academic benchmarks for coding agents tend to reward autonomous task completion, measured by verifiable rewards such as unit-test success. In contrast, real-world coding agents operate with humans in the loop, where success signals are typically noisy, delayed, and sparse. How can we bridge this gap? In this paper, we propose a process to learn a "critic" model from sparse and noisy interaction data, which can then be used both as a reward model for either RL-based training or inference-time scaling. Specifically, we introduce Critic Rubrics, a rubric-based supervision framework with 24 behavioral features that can be derived from human-agent interaction traces alone. Using a semi-supervised objective, we can then jointly predict these rubrics and sparse human feedback (when present). In experiments, we demonstrate that, despite being trained primarily from trace-observable rubrics and sparse real-world outcome proxies, these critics improve best-of-N reranking on SWE-bench (Best@8 +15.9 over Random@8 over the rerankable subset of trajectories), enable early stopping (+17.7 with 83% fewer attempts), and support training-time data curation via critic-selected trajectories.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Critic Rubrics, a framework to learn critic models from sparse/noisy human-agent interaction data for improving coding agents in real-world settings, addressing the gap between academic benchmarks and practical deployment.
AI.motivation: Academic benchmarks for coding agents focus on autonomous task completion with verifiable rewards (like unit-test success), but real-world coding agents operate with humans in the loop where success signals are typically noisy, delayed, and sparse. There's a need to bridge this gap between academic evaluation and practical deployment.
AI.method: Introduces Critic Rubrics, a rubric-based supervision framework with 24 behavioral features derived from human-agent interaction traces. Uses a semi-supervised objective to jointly predict these rubrics and sparse human feedback (when present). The learned critic models can be used as reward models for RL-based training or inference-time scaling.
AI.result: Critics improve best-of-N reranking on SWE-bench (Best@8 +15.9 over Random@8), enable early stopping (+17.7 with 83% fewer attempts), and support training-time data curation via critic-selected trajectories, despite being trained primarily from trace-observable rubrics and sparse real-world outcome proxies.
AI.conclusion: The Critic Rubrics framework successfully bridges the gap between academic benchmarks and real-world coding agent deployment by learning effective critic models from sparse, noisy interaction data, enabling improved performance across multiple practical applications including reranking, early stopping, and data curation.

title: HumanLM: Simulating Users with State Alignment Beats Response Imitation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate how specific users respond to a given context, enabling more user-centric applications that rely on user feedback. However, existing user simulators mostly imitate surface-level patterns and language styles, which fail to reflect the underlying states of real users (e.g., beliefs and emotions). To address these limitations, we propose a novel training framework, HumanLM, which builds user simulators that accurately reflect real users. Our key insight is that, in addition to generating responses, the model should generate natural-language latent states that align with ground-truth responses through reinforcement learning. These latent states correspond to a set of psychologically grounded state dimensions that drive how real users respond. HumanLM further synthesizes these aligned latent states into responses that accurately represent real users. For extensive evaluation, we develop Humanual, a comprehensive benchmark for simulating real users based on public data. Humanual consists of six large-scale datasets with 26k users and 216k responses in total, spanning diverse tasks such as generating user responses to daily life issues, political blogs, and chat sessions with LLM assistants. Across datasets, HumanLM significantly outperforms alternative approaches, achieving an average relative improvement of 16.3% in alignment scores from an LLM judge. In a real-time simulation study with 111 participants, HumanLM achieves the highest similarity to real user responses and competitive human-likeness scores.

AI.tldr: HumanLM is a novel training framework that creates user simulators generating both responses and psychologically-grounded latent states, achieving better alignment with real users than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based user simulators only imitate surface-level patterns and language styles, failing to capture the underlying psychological states (beliefs, emotions) that drive real user responses, limiting their usefulness for user-centric applications.
AI.method: HumanLM trains user simulators to generate both responses and natural-language latent states aligned with ground-truth responses via reinforcement learning. These latent states correspond to psychologically grounded dimensions that drive real user behavior, then synthesized into accurate user representations.
AI.result: HumanLM outperforms alternative approaches across six datasets in the Humanual benchmark (26k users, 216k responses), achieving 16.3% average relative improvement in alignment scores from LLM judges. In a real-time simulation with 111 participants, it achieved highest similarity to real user responses and competitive human-likeness scores.
AI.conclusion: HumanLM successfully addresses limitations of existing user simulators by incorporating psychologically grounded latent states, enabling more accurate simulation of real users' underlying states and responses, which is crucial for developing effective user-centric applications.

title: From Threat Intelligence to Firewall Rules: Semantic Relations in Hybrid AI Agent and Expert System Architectures
summary: Web security demands rapid response capabilities to evolving cyber threats. Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) promises automation, but the need for trustworthy security responses is of the utmost importance. This work investigates the role of semantic relations in extracting information for sensitive operational tasks, such as configuring security controls for mitigating threats. To this end, it proposes to leverage hypernym-hyponym textual relations to extract relevant information from Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) reports. By leveraging a neuro-symbolic approach, the multi-agent system automatically generates CLIPS code for an expert system creating firewall rules to block malicious network traffic. Experimental results show the superior performance of the hypernym-hyponym retrieval strategy compared to various baselines and the higher effectiveness of the agentic approach in mitigating threats.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic multi-agent system uses hypernym-hyponym semantic relations to extract information from CTI reports and automatically generate CLIPS code for firewall rules to block malicious traffic.
AI.motivation: Web security requires rapid response to evolving cyber threats, and while agentic AI promises automation, trustworthy security responses are crucial. The paper aims to investigate how semantic relations can extract information for sensitive operational tasks like configuring security controls.
AI.method: Proposes leveraging hypernym-hyponym textual relations to extract relevant information from Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) reports. Uses a neuro-symbolic approach where a multi-agent system automatically generates CLIPS code for an expert system that creates firewall rules to block malicious network traffic.
AI.result: Experimental results show superior performance of the hypernym-hyponym retrieval strategy compared to various baselines, and demonstrate higher effectiveness of the agentic approach in mitigating threats.
AI.conclusion: The hypernym-hyponym semantic relation extraction approach combined with a neuro-symbolic multi-agent system effectively automates the generation of security controls from CTI reports, providing trustworthy automated threat mitigation.

title: Generative AI in Managerial Decision-Making: Redefining Boundaries through Ambiguity Resolution and Sycophancy Analysis
summary: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly being integrated into complex business workflows, fundamentally shifting the boundaries of managerial decision-making. However, the reliability of its strategic advice in ambiguous business contexts remains a critical knowledge gap. This study addresses this by comparing various models on ambiguity detection, evaluating how a systematic resolution process enhances response quality, and investigating their sycophantic behavior when presented with flawed directives. Using a novel four-dimensional business ambiguity taxonomy, we conducted a human-in-the-loop experiment across strategic, tactical, and operational scenarios. The resulting decisions were assessed with an "LLM-as-a-judge" framework on criteria including agreement, actionability, justification quality, and constraint adherence. Results reveal distinct performance capabilities. While models excel in detecting internal contradictions and contextual ambiguities, they struggle with structural linguistic nuances. Ambiguity resolution consistently increased response quality across all decision types, while sycophantic behavior analysis revealed distinct patterns depending on the model architecture. This study contributes to the bounded rationality literature by positioning GAI as a cognitive scaffold that can detect and resolve ambiguities managers might overlook, but whose own artificial limitations necessitate human management to ensure its reliability as a strategic partner.

AI.tldr: This study examines how generative AI handles business ambiguity, finding it's good at detecting contradictions but struggles with linguistic nuances, and that ambiguity resolution improves response quality while sycophantic behavior varies by model architecture.
AI.motivation: As generative AI becomes integrated into business workflows, there's a critical knowledge gap about its reliability in providing strategic advice in ambiguous business contexts. The study aims to understand how AI models handle business ambiguity and whether they exhibit sycophantic behavior when given flawed directives.
AI.method: The research uses a novel four-dimensional business ambiguity taxonomy and conducts a human-in-the-loop experiment across strategic, tactical, and operational scenarios. Decisions are assessed using an "LLM-as-a-judge" framework evaluating agreement, actionability, justification quality, and constraint adherence.
AI.result: Models excel at detecting internal contradictions and contextual ambiguities but struggle with structural linguistic nuances. Ambiguity resolution consistently improved response quality across all decision types. Sycophantic behavior analysis revealed distinct patterns depending on model architecture.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI can serve as a cognitive scaffold for detecting and resolving ambiguities managers might overlook, but its artificial limitations require human management to ensure reliability as a strategic partner, contributing to bounded rationality literature.

title: TopicENA: Enabling Epistemic Network Analysis at Scale through Automated Topic-Based Coding
summary: Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) is a method for investigating the relational structure of concepts in text by representing co-occurring concepts as networks. Traditional ENA, however, relies heavily on manual expert coding, which limits its scalability and real-world applicability to large text corpora. Topic modeling provides an automated approach to extracting concept-level representations from text and can serve as an alternative to manual coding. To tackle this limitation, the present study merges BERTopic with ENA and introduces TopicENA, a topic-based epistemic network analysis framework. TopicENA substitutes manual concept coding with automatically generated topics while maintaining ENA's capacity for modeling structural associations among concepts. To explain the impact of modeling choices on TopicENA outcomes, three analysis cases are presented. The first case assesses the effect of topic granularity, indicating that coarse-grained topics are preferable for large datasets, whereas fine-grained topics are more effective for smaller datasets. The second case examines topic inclusion thresholds and finds that threshold values should be adjusted according to topic quality indicators to balance network consistency and interpretability. The third case tests TopicENA's scalability by applying it to a substantially larger dataset than those used in previous ENA studies. Collectively, these cases illustrate that TopicENA facilitates practical and interpretable ENA analysis at scale and offers concrete guidance for configuring topic-based ENA pipelines in large-scale text analysis.

AI.tldr: TopicENA combines BERTopic with Epistemic Network Analysis to automate concept extraction and enable scalable network analysis of large text corpora without manual coding.
AI.motivation: Traditional Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) relies on manual expert coding, which limits scalability and real-world applicability to large text corpora. There's a need for automated approaches to extract concept-level representations from text while maintaining ENA's capacity for modeling structural associations among concepts.
AI.method: The study introduces TopicENA, a topic-based epistemic network analysis framework that merges BERTopic with ENA. TopicENA substitutes manual concept coding with automatically generated topics from BERTopic. Three analysis cases are presented to explain the impact of modeling choices: (1) assessing topic granularity effects, (2) examining topic inclusion thresholds, and (3) testing scalability on substantially larger datasets.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Coarse-grained topics are preferable for large datasets, while fine-grained topics work better for smaller datasets; (2) Topic inclusion thresholds should be adjusted according to topic quality indicators to balance network consistency and interpretability; (3) TopicENA successfully scales to substantially larger datasets than previous ENA studies, demonstrating practical applicability for large-scale text analysis.
AI.conclusion: TopicENA facilitates practical and interpretable ENA analysis at scale by automating concept extraction through topic modeling. The framework offers concrete guidance for configuring topic-based ENA pipelines in large-scale text analysis, addressing the scalability limitations of traditional manual coding approaches while maintaining ENA's relational analysis capabilities.

title: Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B Technical Report
summary: We present Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B, a compact open-weight multimodal reasoning model, and share the motivations, design choices, experiments, and learnings that informed its development. Our goal is to contribute practical insight to the research community on building smaller, efficient multimodal reasoning models and to share the result of these learnings as an open-weight model that is good at common vision and language tasks and excels at scientific and mathematical reasoning and understanding user interfaces. Our contributions include demonstrating that careful architecture choices and rigorous data curation enable smaller, open-weight multimodal models to achieve competitive performance with significantly less training and inference-time compute and tokens. The most substantial improvements come from systematic filtering, error correction, and synthetic augmentation -- reinforcing that data quality remains the primary lever for model performance. Systematic ablations show that high-resolution, dynamic-resolution encoders yield consistent improvements, as accurate perception is a prerequisite for high-quality reasoning. Finally, a hybrid mix of reasoning and non-reasoning data with explicit mode tokens allows a single model to deliver fast direct answers for simpler tasks and chain-of-thought reasoning for complex problems.

AI.tldr: Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B is a compact 15B parameter multimodal reasoning model that achieves competitive performance through careful architecture choices and rigorous data curation, excelling at scientific/mathematical reasoning and UI understanding while being efficient in training and inference.
AI.motivation: To contribute practical insights on building smaller, efficient multimodal reasoning models and share an open-weight model that excels at scientific/mathematical reasoning and user interface understanding while being computationally efficient.
AI.method: Combines careful architecture choices with rigorous data curation including systematic filtering, error correction, and synthetic augmentation. Uses high-resolution dynamic-resolution encoders for accurate perception and a hybrid mix of reasoning/non-reasoning data with explicit mode tokens for flexible response generation.
AI.result: Demonstrates that smaller open-weight multimodal models can achieve competitive performance with significantly less training and inference compute through data quality improvements. High-resolution encoders provide consistent improvements, and the hybrid approach enables both fast direct answers and chain-of-thought reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Data quality remains the primary lever for model performance, and careful design choices enable compact multimodal models to excel at complex reasoning tasks while maintaining computational efficiency, providing valuable insights for the research community.

title: Old Habits Die Hard: How Conversational History Geometrically Traps LLMs
summary: How does the conversational past of large language models (LLMs) influence their future performance? Recent work suggests that LLMs are affected by their conversational history in unexpected ways. For instance, hallucinations in prior interactions may influence subsequent model responses. In this work, we introduce History-Echoes, a framework that investigates how conversational history biases subsequent generations. The framework explores this bias from two perspectives: probabilistically, we model conversations as Markov chains to quantify state consistency; geometrically, we measure the consistency of consecutive hidden representations. Across three model families and six datasets spanning diverse phenomena, our analysis reveals a strong correlation between the two perspectives. By bridging these perspectives, we demonstrate that behavioral persistence manifests as a geometric trap, where gaps in the latent space confine the model's trajectory. Code available at https://github.com/technion-cs-nlp/OldHabitsDieHard.

AI.tldr: LLMs' conversational history creates biases in future responses, with hallucinations and prior interactions affecting subsequent generations through probabilistic and geometric consistency measures.
AI.motivation: To understand how LLMs' conversational history influences their future performance, particularly how hallucinations and prior interactions create biases that affect subsequent model responses.
AI.method: History-Echoes framework with two perspectives: probabilistic (modeling conversations as Markov chains to quantify state consistency) and geometric (measuring consistency of consecutive hidden representations).
AI.result: Strong correlation between probabilistic and geometric perspectives across three model families and six datasets; behavioral persistence manifests as a geometric trap where latent space gaps confine model trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Conversational history creates systematic biases in LLM responses, with both probabilistic and geometric analyses revealing consistent patterns of influence that trap models in specific response trajectories.

title: BeamPERL: Parameter-Efficient RL with Verifiable Rewards Specializes Compact LLMs for Structured Beam Mechanics Reasoning
summary: Can reinforcement learning with hard, verifiable rewards teach a compact language model to reason about physics, or does it primarily learn to pattern-match toward correct answers? We study this question by training a 1.5B-parameter reasoning model on beam statics, a classic engineering problem, using parameter-efficient RLVR with binary correctness rewards from symbolic solvers, without teacher-generated reasoning traces. The best BeamPERL checkpoint achieves a 66.7% improvement in Pass@1 over the base model. However, the learned competence is anisotropic: the model generalizes compositionally (more loads) but fails under topological shifts (moved supports) that require the same equilibrium equations. Intermediate checkpoints yield the strongest reasoning, while continued optimization degrades robustness while maintaining reward. These findings reveal a key limitation of outcome-level alignment: reinforcement learning with exact physics rewards induces procedural solution templates rather than internalization of governing equations. The precision of the reward signal - even when analytically exact - does not by itself guarantee transferable physical reasoning. Our results suggest that verifiable rewards may need to be paired with structured reasoning scaffolding to move beyond template matching toward robust scientific reasoning.

AI.tldr: Reinforcement learning with exact physics rewards teaches language models procedural templates rather than true physical reasoning, showing limited transfer despite binary correctness rewards from symbolic solvers.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether reinforcement learning with hard, verifiable rewards can teach compact language models to reason about physics or if they primarily learn to pattern-match toward correct answers.
AI.method: Trained a 1.5B-parameter reasoning model on beam statics using parameter-efficient RLVR with binary correctness rewards from symbolic solvers, without teacher-generated reasoning traces.
AI.result: Best checkpoint achieved 66.7% improvement in Pass@1 over base model, but learned competence is anisotropic: generalizes compositionally (more loads) but fails under topological shifts (moved supports). Intermediate checkpoints yield strongest reasoning, while continued optimization degrades robustness while maintaining reward.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning with exact physics rewards induces procedural solution templates rather than internalization of governing equations. Verifiable rewards may need to be paired with structured reasoning scaffolding to move beyond template matching toward robust scientific reasoning.

title: Combating data scarcity in recommendation services: Integrating cognitive types of VARK and neural network technologies (LLM)
summary: Cold start scenarios present fundamental obstacles to effective recommendation generation, particularly when dealing with users lacking interaction history or items with sparse metadata. This research proposes an innovative hybrid framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) for content semantic analysis and knowledge graph development, integrated with cognitive profiling based on VARK (Visual, Auditory, Reading/Writing, Kinesthetic) learning preferences. The proposed system tackles multiple cold start dimensions: enriching inadequate item descriptions through LLM processing, generating user profiles from minimal data, and dynamically adjusting presentation formats based on cognitive assessment. The framework comprises six integrated components: semantic metadata enhancement, dynamic graph construction, VARK-based profiling, mental state estimation, graph-enhanced retrieval with LLM-powered ranking, and adaptive interface design with iterative learning. Experimental validation on MovieLens-1M dataset demonstrates the system's capacity for personalized recommendation generation despite limited initial information. This work establishes groundwork for cognitively-aware recommendation systems capable of overcoming cold start limitations through semantic comprehension and psychological modeling, offering personalized, explainable recommendations from initial user contact.

AI.tldr: Hybrid framework combining LLMs for semantic analysis and VARK learning preferences to address cold start recommendation problems through content enrichment, user profiling, and adaptive presentation.
AI.motivation: Cold start scenarios create fundamental obstacles for recommendation systems, especially when dealing with users lacking interaction history or items with sparse metadata. Traditional approaches struggle with inadequate information for effective personalization.
AI.method: Proposes a hybrid framework with six integrated components: 1) semantic metadata enhancement using LLMs, 2) dynamic knowledge graph construction, 3) VARK-based cognitive profiling, 4) mental state estimation, 5) graph-enhanced retrieval with LLM-powered ranking, and 6) adaptive interface design with iterative learning.
AI.result: Experimental validation on MovieLens-1M dataset demonstrates the system's capacity for personalized recommendation generation despite limited initial information. The framework successfully addresses multiple cold start dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Establishes groundwork for cognitively-aware recommendation systems capable of overcoming cold start limitations through semantic comprehension and psychological modeling, offering personalized, explainable recommendations from initial user contact.

title: Towards Realistic Personalization: Evaluating Long-Horizon Preference Following in Personalized User-LLM Interactions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly serving as personal assistants, where users share complex and diverse preferences over extended interactions. However, assessing how well LLMs can follow these preferences in realistic, long-term situations remains underexplored. This work proposes RealPref, a benchmark for evaluating realistic preference-following in personalized user-LLM interactions. RealPref features 100 user profiles, 1300 personalized preferences, four types of preference expression (ranging from explicit to implicit), and long-horizon interaction histories. It includes three types of test questions (multiple-choice, true-or-false, and open-ended), with detailed rubrics for LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. Results indicate that LLM performance significantly drops as context length grows and preference expression becomes more implicit, and that generalizing user preference understanding to unseen scenarios poses further challenges. RealPref and these findings provide a foundation for future research to develop user-aware LLM assistants that better adapt to individual needs. The code is available at https://github.com/GG14127/RealPref.

AI.tldr: RealPref is a benchmark for evaluating how well LLMs follow user preferences in realistic, long-term personalized interactions, featuring 100 user profiles, 1300 preferences, and various preference expression types, with findings showing performance declines as context grows and preferences become more implicit.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as personal assistants that need to understand and follow complex user preferences over extended interactions, but there's a lack of benchmarks to evaluate this capability in realistic, long-term scenarios.
AI.method: Developed RealPref benchmark with 100 user profiles, 1300 personalized preferences, four types of preference expression (explicit to implicit), long-horizon interaction histories, and three test question types (multiple-choice, true-or-false, open-ended) with detailed rubrics for LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.
AI.result: LLM performance significantly decreases as context length increases and preference expression becomes more implicit; generalizing user preference understanding to unseen scenarios presents additional challenges.
AI.conclusion: RealPref provides a foundation for developing user-aware LLM assistants that better adapt to individual needs, highlighting the need for improved long-term preference understanding and generalization capabilities.

title: Entropic-Time Inference: Self-Organizing Large Language Model Decoding Beyond Attention
summary: Modern large language model (LLM) inference engines optimize throughput and latency under fixed decoding rules, treating generation as a linear progression in token time. We propose a fundamentally different paradigm: entropic\-time inference, where decoding is governed by the flow of uncertainty rather than token index. We introduce a self\-organizing inference architecture that jointly couples scheduling, attention sparsification, and sampling temperature under a unified entropy control objective. Our method extends vLLM with entropy-aware scheduling, entropic pruning of paged attention blocks, and adaptive temperature control that stabilizes generation near a target entropy regime. This transforms inference into a resource\-intelligent thermodynamic process that allocates computation where uncertainty reduction is maximized. We present a concrete systems design, pseudocode, and integration plan, demonstrating how entropy can serve as a first\-class control signal for scalable LLM inference.

AI.tldr: Entropic-time inference paradigm treats LLM decoding as uncertainty flow rather than token progression, introducing entropy-aware scheduling, attention pruning, and temperature control for resource-intelligent generation.
AI.motivation: Current LLM inference engines optimize throughput/latency under fixed decoding rules, treating generation as linear token progression. This fails to leverage the fundamental role of uncertainty in generation quality and computational efficiency.
AI.method: Self-organizing inference architecture with: 1) entropy-aware scheduling that prioritizes uncertain sequences, 2) entropic pruning of paged attention blocks based on uncertainty reduction, and 3) adaptive temperature control stabilizing generation near target entropy regime. Built as extension to vLLM with unified entropy control objective.
AI.result: Transforms inference into resource-intelligent thermodynamic process allocating computation where uncertainty reduction is maximized. Provides concrete systems design, pseudocode, and integration plan demonstrating entropy as first-class control signal for scalable LLM inference.
AI.conclusion: Entropy can serve as fundamental control signal for LLM inference, enabling more efficient computation allocation based on uncertainty flow rather than token progression, potentially improving both efficiency and generation quality.

title: Agentics 2.0: Logical Transduction Algebra for Agentic Data Workflows
summary: Agentic AI is rapidly transitioning from research prototypes to enterprise deployments, where requirements extend to meet the software quality attributes of reliability, scalability, and observability beyond plausible text generation. We present Agentics 2.0, a lightweight, Python-native framework for building high-quality, structured, explainable, and type-safe agentic data workflows. At the core of Agentics 2.0, the logical transduction algebra formalizes a large language model inference call as a typed semantic transformation, which we call a transducible function that enforces schema validity and the locality of evidence. The transducible functions compose into larger programs via algebraically grounded operators and execute as stateless asynchronous calls in parallel in asynchronous Map-Reduce programs. The proposed framework provides semantic reliability through strong typing, semantic observability through evidence tracing between slots of the input and output types, and scalability through stateless parallel execution. We instantiate reusable design patterns and evaluate the programs in Agentics 2.0 on challenging benchmarks, including DiscoveryBench for data-driven discovery and Archer for NL-to-SQL semantic parsing, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: Agentics 2.0 is a Python-native framework for building reliable, scalable, and observable agentic AI workflows using typed semantic transformations called transducible functions.
AI.motivation: Enterprise deployments of agentic AI require software quality attributes like reliability, scalability, and observability beyond just plausible text generation, which existing research prototypes often lack.
AI.method: Introduces logical transduction algebra that formalizes LLM inference as typed semantic transformations (transducible functions) with schema validity and evidence locality. These functions compose via algebraic operators and execute as stateless asynchronous calls in parallel Map-Reduce programs.
AI.result: Demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on challenging benchmarks including DiscoveryBench for data-driven discovery and Archer for NL-to-SQL semantic parsing, with reusable design patterns.
AI.conclusion: Agentics 2.0 provides a lightweight framework for building high-quality agentic workflows with semantic reliability through strong typing, semantic observability through evidence tracing, and scalability through stateless parallel execution.

title: The Logovista English--Japanese Machine Translation System
summary:
This paper documents the architecture, development practices, and preserved artifacts of the Logovista English--Japanese machine translation system, a large, explicitly rule-based MT system that was developed and sold commercially from the early 1990s through at least 2012. The system combined hand-authored grammatical rules, a large central dictionary encoding syntactic and semantic constraints, and chart-based parsing with weighted interpretation scoring to manage extensive structural ambiguity.
  The account emphasizes how the system was extended and maintained under real-world usage pressures, including regression control, ambiguity management, and the limits encountered as coverage expanded. Unlike many rule-based MT systems described primarily in research settings, Logovista was deployed for decades and evolved continuously in response to practical requirements. The paper is intended as a technical and historical record rather than an argument for reviving rule-based MT, and describes the software and linguistic resources that have been preserved for potential future study.

AI.tldr: Logovista was a commercial rule-based English-Japanese MT system (1990s-2012) combining hand-authored grammar rules, large constraint dictionaries, and chart parsing with scoring to manage ambiguity, maintained continuously under real-world usage.
AI.motivation: To document the architecture, development practices, and preserved artifacts of Logovista, a commercially deployed rule-based MT system that operated for decades, providing a technical and historical record of a practical, continuously evolving system rather than advocating for rule-based MT revival.
AI.method: Combined hand-authored grammatical rules, a large central dictionary encoding syntactic and semantic constraints, and chart-based parsing with weighted interpretation scoring to manage extensive structural ambiguity. Emphasized real-world maintenance practices including regression control and ambiguity management.
AI.result: Successfully deployed commercially from early 1990s through at least 2012, continuously evolved in response to practical requirements, and preserved software/linguistic resources for future study. Demonstrated limits encountered as coverage expanded.
AI.conclusion: Provides valuable technical and historical documentation of a commercially successful rule-based MT system that operated for decades, offering insights into practical maintenance, evolution, and preservation of such systems, serving as a record rather than an argument for rule-based MT revival.

title: $τ$-Knowledge: Evaluating Conversational Agents over Unstructured Knowledge
summary: Conversational agents are increasingly deployed in knowledge-intensive settings, where correct behavior depends on retrieving and applying domain-specific knowledge from large, proprietary, and unstructured corpora during live interactions with users. Yet most existing benchmarks evaluate retrieval or tool use independently of each other, creating a gap in realistic, fully agentic evaluation over unstructured data in long-horizon interactions. We introduce $τ$-Knowledge, an extension of $τ$-Bench for evaluating agents in environments where success depends on coordinating external, natural-language knowledge with tool outputs to produce verifiable, policy-compliant state changes. Our new domain, $τ$-Banking, models realistic fintech customer support workflows in which agents must navigate roughly 700 interconnected knowledge documents while executing tool-mediated account updates. Across embedding-based retrieval and terminal-based search, even frontier models with high reasoning budgets achieve only $\sim$25.5% pass^1, with reliability degrading sharply over repeated trials. Agents struggle to retrieve the correct documents from densely interlinked knowledge bases and to reason accurately over complex internal policies. Overall, $τ$-Knowledge provides a realistic testbed for developing agents that integrate unstructured knowledge in human-facing deployments.

AI.tldr: τ-Knowledge extends τ-Bench to evaluate conversational agents that must coordinate external natural-language knowledge with tool outputs for policy-compliant state changes in knowledge-intensive domains like fintech customer support.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate retrieval or tool use independently, creating a gap in realistic agent evaluation over unstructured data in long-horizon interactions where agents must retrieve and apply domain-specific knowledge from large proprietary corpora during live user interactions.
AI.method: Introduces τ-Knowledge as an extension of τ-Bench, with a new domain called τ-Banking that models realistic fintech customer support workflows. Agents must navigate ~700 interconnected knowledge documents while executing tool-mediated account updates, testing coordination of external knowledge retrieval with tool outputs.
AI.result: Even frontier models with high reasoning budgets achieve only ~25.5% pass rate across embedding-based retrieval and terminal-based search. Reliability degrades sharply over repeated trials. Agents struggle with retrieving correct documents from densely interlinked knowledge bases and reasoning accurately over complex internal policies.
AI.conclusion: τ-Knowledge provides a realistic testbed for developing agents that integrate unstructured knowledge in human-facing deployments, highlighting significant challenges in coordinating knowledge retrieval with tool use for policy-compliant state changes.

title: Escaping the BLEU Trap: A Signal-Grounded Framework with Decoupled Semantic Guidance for EEG-to-Text Decoding
summary: Decoding natural language from non-invasive EEG signals is a promising yet challenging task. However, current state-of-the-art models remain constrained by three fundamental limitations: Semantic Bias (mode collapse into generic templates), Signal Neglect (hallucination based on linguistic priors rather than neural inputs), and the BLEU Trap, where evaluation metrics are artificially inflated by high-frequency stopwords, masking a lack of true semantic fidelity. To address these challenges, we propose SemKey, a novel multi-stage framework that enforces signal-grounded generation through four decoupled semantic objectives: sentiment, topic, length, and surprisal. We redesign the interaction between the neural encoder and the Large Language Model (LLM) by injecting semantic prompts as Queries and EEG embeddings as Key-Value pairs, strictly forcing the model to attend to neural inputs. Furthermore, we move beyond standard translation metrics by adopting N-way Retrieval Accuracy and Fréchet Distance to rigorously assess diversity and alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach effectively eliminates hallucinations on noise inputs and achieves SOTA performance on these robust protocols. Code will be released upon acceptance at https://github.com/xmed-lab/SemKey.

AI.tldr: SemKey is a multi-stage EEG-to-text decoding framework that addresses semantic bias, signal neglect, and BLEU trap limitations through semantic prompting and robust evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Current EEG-to-text models suffer from three fundamental limitations: Semantic Bias (mode collapse into generic templates), Signal Neglect (hallucination based on linguistic priors rather than neural inputs), and the BLEU Trap (inflated metrics from high-frequency stopwords masking poor semantic fidelity).
AI.method: Proposes SemKey, a multi-stage framework with four decoupled semantic objectives (sentiment, topic, length, surprisal). Redesigns neural encoder-LLM interaction by injecting semantic prompts as Queries and EEG embeddings as Key-Value pairs to force attention to neural inputs. Uses N-way Retrieval Accuracy and Fréchet Distance for evaluation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the approach effectively eliminates hallucinations on noise inputs and achieves state-of-the-art performance on robust evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: SemKey addresses key limitations in EEG-to-text decoding through signal-grounded generation and rigorous evaluation, demonstrating improved semantic fidelity and reduced hallucinations.

title: A Dual-Helix Governance Approach Towards Reliable Agentic AI for WebGIS Development
comment: Paper submitted to Transactions in GIS
summary: WebGIS development requires rigor, yet agentic AI frequently fails due to five large language model (LLM) limitations: context constraints, cross-session forgetting, stochasticity, instruction failure, and adaptation rigidity. We propose a dual-helix governance framework reframing these challenges as structural governance problems that model capacity alone cannot resolve. We implement the framework as a 3-track architecture (Knowledge, Behavior, Skills) that uses a knowledge graph substrate to stabilize execution by externalizing domain facts and enforcing executable protocols, complemented by a self-learning cycle for autonomous knowledge growth. Applying this to the FutureShorelines WebGIS tool, a governed agent refactored a 2,265-line monolithic codebase into modular ES6 components. Results demonstrated a 51\% reduction in cyclomatic complexity and a 7-point increase in maintainability index. A comparative experiment against a zero-shot LLM confirms that externalized governance, not just model capability, drives operational reliability in geospatial engineering. This approach is implemented in the open-source AgentLoom governance toolkit.

AI.tldr: A dual-helix governance framework addresses LLM limitations in WebGIS development by externalizing domain knowledge and protocols, achieving significant code quality improvements through structured agent governance.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI frequently fails in WebGIS development due to five key LLM limitations: context constraints, cross-session forgetting, stochasticity, instruction failure, and adaptation rigidity. These limitations prevent reliable application of AI agents in rigorous geospatial engineering contexts.
AI.method: Proposed a dual-helix governance framework reframing LLM challenges as structural governance problems. Implemented as a 3-track architecture (Knowledge, Behavior, Skills) using a knowledge graph substrate to externalize domain facts and enforce executable protocols, complemented by a self-learning cycle for autonomous knowledge growth. Applied to the FutureShorelines WebGIS tool.
AI.result: A governed agent successfully refactored a 2,265-line monolithic codebase into modular ES6 components, achieving a 51% reduction in cyclomatic complexity and a 7-point increase in maintainability index. Comparative experiments against zero-shot LLM confirmed that externalized governance, not just model capability, drives operational reliability.
AI.conclusion: The dual-helix governance framework effectively addresses LLM limitations in WebGIS development by externalizing governance structures. The approach demonstrates that structured governance, not just model capacity, is essential for reliable agentic AI in geospatial engineering. The framework is available as the open-source AgentLoom governance toolkit.

title: How does fine-tuning improve sensorimotor representations in large language models?
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a significant "embodiment gap", where their text-based representations fail to align with human sensorimotor experiences. This study systematically investigates whether and how task-specific fine-tuning can bridge this gap. Utilizing Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and dimension-specific correlation metrics, we demonstrate that the internal representations of LLMs can be steered toward more embodied, grounded patterns through fine-tuning. Furthermore, the results show that while sensorimotor improvements generalize robustly across languages and related sensory-motor dimensions, they are highly sensitive to the learning objective, failing to transfer across two disparate task formats.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs on sensorimotor tasks can bridge the embodiment gap by steering internal representations toward more grounded patterns, but improvements are task-specific and don't transfer across disparate formats.
AI.motivation: LLMs have an "embodiment gap" where their text-based representations don't align with human sensorimotor experiences. The study investigates whether task-specific fine-tuning can bridge this gap and make LLM representations more embodied.
AI.method: Used Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and dimension-specific correlation metrics to analyze how fine-tuning affects LLM representations. Systematically investigated whether task-specific fine-tuning can steer internal representations toward more embodied patterns.
AI.result: Fine-tuning successfully steers LLM internal representations toward more embodied, grounded patterns. Sensorimotor improvements generalize robustly across languages and related sensory-motor dimensions, but are highly sensitive to learning objectives and fail to transfer across two disparate task formats.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific fine-tuning can effectively bridge the embodiment gap in LLMs by making their representations more aligned with human sensorimotor experiences, but the improvements are task-specific and don't generalize across fundamentally different task formats.

title: Towards Self-Robust LLMs: Intrinsic Prompt Noise Resistance via CoIPO
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable and steadily improving performance across a wide range of tasks. However, LLM performance may be highly sensitive to prompt variations especially in scenarios with limited openness or strict output formatting requirements, indicating insufficient robustness. In real-world applications, user prompts provided to LLMs often contain imperfections, which may undermine the quality of the model's responses. To address this issue, previous work has primarily focused on preprocessing prompts, employing external tools or even LLMs to refine prompt formulations in advance. However, these approaches overlook the intrinsic robustness of LLMs, and their reliance on external components introduces additional computational overhead and uncertainty. In this work, we propose a Contrastive Learning-based Inverse Direct Preference Optimization (CoIPO) method that minimizes the discrepancy between the label-aligned logits produced by the model under a clean prompt and its noisy counterpart, and conduct a detailed analysis using mutual information theory. We augment the FLAN dataset by constructing paired prompts, each consisting of a clean prompt and its corresponding noisy version for training. Additionally, to evaluate the effectiveness, we develop NoisyPromptBench, a benchmark enhanced and derived from the existing PromptBench. Experimental results conducted on NoisyPromptBench demonstrate that our proposed method achieves a significant improvement in average accuracy over the current state-of-the-art approaches. The source code of CoIPO, pair-wise FLAN datasets, and NoisyPromptBench have already been released on https://github.com/vegetable-yx/CoIPO.

AI.tldr: CoIPO is a contrastive learning-based inverse direct preference optimization method that improves LLM robustness to noisy prompts by minimizing logit discrepancies between clean and noisy prompt responses, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the NoisyPromptBench benchmark.
AI.motivation: LLMs show remarkable performance but are highly sensitive to prompt variations, especially in scenarios with limited openness or strict formatting requirements. Real-world user prompts often contain imperfections that degrade response quality. Existing approaches focus on preprocessing prompts using external tools or LLMs, which overlooks intrinsic model robustness and introduces computational overhead and uncertainty.
AI.method: Proposes Contrastive Learning-based Inverse Direct Preference Optimization (CoIPO) that minimizes the discrepancy between label-aligned logits produced by the model under clean prompts and their noisy counterparts. Uses mutual information theory for analysis. Augments FLAN dataset with paired prompts (clean + noisy versions) for training. Develops NoisyPromptBench benchmark derived from PromptBench for evaluation.
AI.result: Experimental results on NoisyPromptBench demonstrate significant improvement in average accuracy over current state-of-the-art approaches. The method, datasets, and benchmark are publicly released on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: CoIPO effectively enhances LLM robustness to noisy prompts by leveraging contrastive learning and inverse direct preference optimization, addressing limitations of external preprocessing approaches while improving model intrinsic robustness without additional computational overhead.

title: M-QUEST -- Meme Question-Understanding Evaluation on Semantics and Toxicity
summary: Internet memes are a powerful form of online communication, yet their nature and reliance on commonsense knowledge make toxicity detection challenging. Identifying key features for meme interpretation and understanding, is a crucial task. Previous work has been focused on some elements contributing to the meaning, such as the Textual dimension via OCR, the Visual dimension via object recognition, upper layers of meaning like the Emotional dimension, Toxicity detection via proxy variables, such as hate speech detection, and sentiment analysis. Nevertheless, there is still a lack of an overall architecture able to formally identify elements contributing to the meaning of a meme, and be used in the sense-making process. In this work, we present a semantic framework and a corresponding benchmark for automatic knowledge extraction from memes. First, we identify the necessary dimensions to understand and interpret a meme: Textual material, Visual material, Scene, Background Knowledge, Emotion, Semiotic Projection, Analogical Mapping, Overall Intent, Target Community, and Toxicity Assessment. Second, the framework guides a semi-automatic process of generating a benchmark with commonsense question-answer pairs about meme toxicity assessment and its underlying reason. The resulting benchmark M-QUEST consists of 609 question-answer pairs for 307 memes. Thirdly, we evaluate eight open-source large language models on their ability to correctly solve M-QUEST. Our results show that current models' commonsense reasoning capabilities for toxic meme interpretation vary depending on the dimension and architecture. Models with instruction tuning and reasoning capabilities significantly outperform the others, though pragmatic inference questions remain challenging. We release code, benchmark, and prompts to support future research intersecting multimodal content safety and commonsense reasoning.

AI.tldr: Proposes M-QUEST: a semantic framework and benchmark for toxic meme interpretation via commonsense reasoning, evaluating LLMs on 609 QA pairs across 10 dimensions.
AI.motivation: Internet memes are challenging for toxicity detection due to their reliance on commonsense knowledge and multimodal nature. Previous work focused on isolated dimensions (text, visual, emotion, toxicity proxies) but lacked a comprehensive framework for formal meme interpretation and sense-making.
AI.method: 1) Developed a semantic framework identifying 10 dimensions for meme understanding: Textual material, Visual material, Scene, Background Knowledge, Emotion, Semiotic Projection, Analogical Mapping, Overall Intent, Target Community, and Toxicity Assessment. 2) Created M-QUEST benchmark through semi-automatic generation of 609 question-answer pairs for 307 memes. 3) Evaluated 8 open-source LLMs on their ability to solve M-QUEST questions.
AI.result: Models with instruction tuning and reasoning capabilities significantly outperform others. Performance varies across dimensions and architectures. Pragmatic inference questions remain particularly challenging for current models.
AI.conclusion: The M-QUEST framework and benchmark provide a comprehensive approach to toxic meme interpretation via commonsense reasoning. While instruction-tuned models show promise, significant challenges remain in pragmatic inference. The released resources support future research at the intersection of multimodal content safety and commonsense reasoning.

title: The Influence of Iconicity in Transfer Learning for Sign Language Recognition
summary: Most sign language recognition research relies on Transfer Learning (TL) from vision-based datasets such as ImageNet. Some extend this to alternatively available language datasets, often focusing on signs with cross-linguistic similarities. This body of work examines the necessity of these likenesses on effective knowledge transfer by comparing TL performance between iconic signs of two different sign language pairs: Chinese to Arabic and Greek to Flemish. Google Mediapipe was utilised as an input feature extractor, enabling spatial information of these signs to be processed with a Multilayer Perceptron architecture and the temporal information with a Gated Recurrent Unit. Experimental results showed a 7.02% improvement for Arabic and 1.07% for Flemish when conducting iconic TL from Chinese and Greek respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper examines whether cross-linguistic similarities between sign languages are necessary for effective transfer learning, comparing performance between Chinese-Arabic and Greek-Flemish sign language pairs using Mediapipe feature extraction and GRU-based temporal modeling.
AI.motivation: Most sign language recognition research relies on transfer learning from vision datasets like ImageNet, with some extending to language datasets focusing on signs with cross-linguistic similarities. The paper investigates whether these likenesses are actually necessary for effective knowledge transfer between different sign languages.
AI.method: Used Google Mediapipe as input feature extractor to capture spatial information of signs. Processed spatial features with a Multilayer Perceptron architecture and temporal information with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). Compared transfer learning performance between two sign language pairs: Chinese to Arabic and Greek to Flemish, focusing on iconic signs.
AI.result: Experimental results showed 7.02% improvement for Arabic when conducting transfer learning from Chinese, and 1.07% improvement for Flemish when transferring from Greek. This demonstrates that effective knowledge transfer can occur even between sign languages without obvious cross-linguistic similarities.
AI.conclusion: Cross-linguistic similarities between sign languages are not strictly necessary for effective transfer learning. Knowledge transfer can be beneficial even between linguistically distant sign language pairs, as evidenced by the performance improvements observed in both Chinese-Arabic and Greek-Flemish transfers.

title: Retcon -- a Prompt-Based Technique for Precise Control of LLMs in Conversations
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 appendixes with prompts and examples
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) allow agents to execute complex natural language tasks. Many LLM applications, such as support agents, teaching assistants, and interactive bots, involve multi-turn conversations. However, it remains challenging to control LLMs in the context of such interactions, particularly when the LLM behavior needs to be adjustable over the course of the conversation. In this paper, we present Retcon, a few-shot prompting technique designed to provide turn-level control over LLMs in conversations. We then demonstrate that it performs significantly better than zero-shot and traditional few-shot prompting.

AI.tldr: Retcon is a few-shot prompting technique that provides turn-level control over LLMs in multi-turn conversations, outperforming zero-shot and traditional few-shot methods.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in multi-turn conversational applications (support agents, teaching assistants, interactive bots), but controlling their behavior at the turn level during conversations remains challenging, especially when behavior needs adjustment over the course of interaction.
AI.method: Retcon is a few-shot prompting technique designed specifically for turn-level control in conversations. It likely involves providing examples of desired conversational behaviors at each turn, enabling fine-grained control over LLM responses throughout multi-turn interactions.
AI.result: Retcon performs significantly better than both zero-shot prompting and traditional few-shot prompting methods for controlling LLMs in conversational contexts.
AI.conclusion: Retcon provides an effective solution for turn-level control of LLMs in multi-turn conversations, addressing a key challenge in deploying LLMs for interactive applications where behavior needs to be adjustable throughout the conversation.

title: Quantum-Inspired Self-Attention in a Large Language Model
summary: Recent advances in Natural Language Processing have been predominantly driven by transformer-based architectures, which rely heavily on self-attention mechanisms to model relationships between tokens in a sequence. Similarly, the field of Quantum Natural Language Processing, which seeks to leverage quantum principles to address challenges in language understanding and generation tasks, has seen the recent development of quantum self-attention mechanisms. We propose a classical quantum-inspired self-attention (QISA) mechanism and integrate it into the full autoregressive language modeling pipeline of GPT-1. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first integration of this kind, as previous quantum self-attention mechanisms have been primarily tested on text classification. In our experiments, QISA achieves better performance when compared to standard self-attention on the metrics character error rate ($15.5\times$ better), word error rate ($4.7 \times $) and cross-entropy loss ($13 \times$). This is achieved while only requiring a $ 2.6\times$ longer inference time.

AI.tldr: Classical quantum-inspired self-attention (QISA) integrated into GPT-1 achieves significantly better performance on language modeling metrics with only moderate inference time increase.
AI.motivation: While quantum self-attention mechanisms have been developed for QNLP, they've only been tested on text classification tasks. The authors aim to integrate quantum-inspired self-attention into full autoregressive language modeling to explore its potential benefits.
AI.method: Proposed a classical quantum-inspired self-attention (QISA) mechanism and integrated it into the GPT-1 architecture, creating the first integration of quantum-inspired self-attention into a full autoregressive language modeling pipeline.
AI.result: QISA outperformed standard self-attention with 15.5× better character error rate, 4.7× better word error rate, and 13× better cross-entropy loss, while requiring only 2.6× longer inference time.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-inspired self-attention mechanisms can significantly improve language modeling performance with reasonable computational overhead, demonstrating the potential of quantum-inspired approaches in classical NLP architectures.

title: Automated Concept Discovery for LLM-as-a-Judge Preference Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as scalable evaluators of model outputs, but their preference judgments exhibit systematic biases and can diverge from human evaluations. Prior work on LLM-as-a-judge has largely focused on a small, predefined set of hypothesized biases, leaving open the problem of automatically discovering unknown drivers of LLM preferences. We address this gap by studying several embedding-level concept extraction methods for analyzing LLM judge behavior. We compare these methods in terms of interpretability and predictiveness, finding that sparse autoencoder-based approaches recover substantially more interpretable preference features than alternatives while remaining competitive in predicting LLM decisions. Using over 27k paired responses from multiple human preference datasets and judgments from three LLMs, we analyze LLM judgments and compare them to those of human annotators. Our method both validates existing results, such as the tendency for LLMs to prefer refusal of sensitive requests at higher rates than humans, and uncovers new trends across both general and domain-specific datasets, including biases toward responses that emphasize concreteness and empathy in approaching new situations, toward detail and formality in academic advice, and against legal guidance that promotes active steps like calling police and filing lawsuits. Our results show that automated concept discovery enables systematic analysis of LLM judge preferences without predefined bias taxonomies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces automated concept extraction methods to discover unknown biases in LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, finding sparse autoencoders recover interpretable preference features while validating known biases and uncovering new ones across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as scalable evaluators, but their preference judgments exhibit systematic biases that may diverge from human evaluations. Prior work focused on predefined bias sets, leaving the problem of automatically discovering unknown drivers of LLM preferences unaddressed.
AI.method: The study compares several embedding-level concept extraction methods for analyzing LLM judge behavior, with sparse autoencoder-based approaches showing superior interpretability. Analysis uses over 27k paired responses from multiple human preference datasets and judgments from three LLMs.
AI.result: Sparse autoencoder-based approaches recover substantially more interpretable preference features than alternatives while remaining competitive in predicting LLM decisions. The method validates existing results (e.g., LLMs preferring refusal of sensitive requests) and uncovers new biases: toward responses emphasizing concreteness and empathy, detail and formality in academic advice, and against legal guidance promoting active steps.
AI.conclusion: Automated concept discovery enables systematic analysis of LLM judge preferences without predefined bias taxonomies, providing a scalable approach to understanding and potentially mitigating systematic biases in LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.

title: From We to Me: Theory Informed Narrative Shift with Abductive Reasoning
summary: Effective communication often relies on aligning a message with an audience's narrative and worldview. Narrative shift involves transforming text to reflect a different narrative framework while preserving its original core message--a task we demonstrate is significantly challenging for current Large Language Models (LLMs). To address this, we propose a neurosymbolic approach grounded in social science theory and abductive reasoning. Our method automatically extracts rules to abduce the specific story elements needed to guide an LLM through a consistent and targeted narrative transformation. Across multiple LLMs, abduction-guided transformed stories shifted the narrative while maintaining the fidelity with the original story. For example, with GPT-4o we outperform the zero-shot LLM baseline by 55.88% for collectivistic to individualistic narrative shift while maintaining superior semantic similarity with the original stories (40.4% improvement in KL divergence). For individualistic to collectivistic transformation, we achieve comparable improvements. We show similar performance across both directions for Llama-4, and Grok-4 and competitive performance for Deepseek-R1.

AI.tldr: Proposes a neurosymbolic approach using social science theory and abductive reasoning to transform text between different narrative frameworks (individualistic vs. collectivistic) while preserving core message, significantly outperforming zero-shot LLM baselines.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs struggle with narrative shift—transforming text to reflect different narrative frameworks while preserving core messages. Effective communication requires aligning messages with audience's worldview, making this a critical capability gap.
AI.method: Neurosymbolic approach combining social science theory with abductive reasoning. Automatically extracts rules to abduce specific story elements needed for consistent narrative transformation. Uses abduction-guided process to steer LLMs through targeted narrative shifts.
AI.result: Significant improvements over zero-shot LLM baselines: 55.88% better for collectivistic→individualistic shift with GPT-4o, plus 40.4% improvement in semantic similarity (KL divergence). Comparable improvements for individualistic→collectivistic direction. Consistent performance across GPT-4o, Llama-4, Grok-4, and competitive with Deepseek-R1.
AI.conclusion: Abduction-guided neurosymbolic approach effectively addresses LLMs' narrative shift limitations, enabling consistent narrative transformations while maintaining message fidelity. Demonstrates value of integrating social science theory with computational methods for complex text adaptation tasks.

title: DIALEVAL: Automated Type-Theoretic Evaluation of LLM Instruction Following
summary: Evaluating instruction following in Large Language Models requires decomposing instructions into verifiable requirements and assessing satisfaction--tasks currently dependent on manual annotation and uniform criteria that do not align with human judgment patterns. We present DIALEVAL, a type-theoretic framework using dual LLM agents to automate instruction decomposition into typed predicates and implement type-specific satisfaction semantics. The framework enforces formal atomicity and independence constraints during automated extraction, then applies differentiated evaluation criteria--semantic equivalence for content predicates, exact precision for numerical predicates--mirroring empirically observed human assessment patterns. Extended to multi-turn dialogues through history-aware satisfaction functions, DIALEVAL enables evaluation in conversational contexts where single-turn methods fail. Validation demonstrates 90.38% accuracy (26.45% error reduction over baselines) and substantially stronger correlation with human judgment for complex instructions.

AI.tldr: DIALEVAL is a type-theoretic framework using dual LLM agents to automate instruction decomposition and evaluation, achieving 90.38% accuracy with 26.45% error reduction over baselines.
AI.motivation: Current instruction following evaluation in LLMs relies on manual annotation and uniform criteria that don't align with human judgment patterns, requiring automated decomposition and type-specific evaluation.
AI.method: Uses dual LLM agents to decompose instructions into typed predicates with formal atomicity/independence constraints, then applies type-specific satisfaction semantics (semantic equivalence for content, exact precision for numerical). Extended to multi-turn dialogues via history-aware satisfaction functions.
AI.result: Achieves 90.38% accuracy with 26.45% error reduction over baselines, shows substantially stronger correlation with human judgment for complex instructions, and enables evaluation in conversational contexts.
AI.conclusion: DIALEVAL provides an automated, type-theoretic framework that better aligns with human judgment patterns for instruction following evaluation, extending effectively to multi-turn dialogue contexts.

title: Can Large Language Models Derive New Knowledge? A Dynamic Benchmark for Biological Knowledge Discovery
summary: Recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable potential in automatic knowledge discovery. However, rigorously evaluating an AI's capacity for knowledge discovery remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks predominantly rely on static datasets, leading to inevitable data contamination where models have likely seen the evaluation knowledge during training. Furthermore, the rapid release cycles of modern LLMs render static benchmarks quickly outdated, failing to assess the ability to discover truly new knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose DBench-Bio, a dynamic and fully automated benchmark designed to evaluate AI's biological knowledge discovery ability. DBench-Bio employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) data acquisition of rigorous, authoritative paper abstracts; (2) QA extraction utilizing LLMs to synthesize scientific hypothesis questions and corresponding discovery answers; and (3) QA filter to ensure quality based on relevance, clarity, and centrality. We instantiate this pipeline to construct a monthly-updated benchmark covering 12 biomedical sub-domains. Extensive evaluations of SOTA models reveal current limitations in discovering new knowledge. Our work provides the first dynamic, automatic framework for assessing the new knowledge discovery capabilities of AI systems, establishing a living, evolving resource for AI research community to catalyze the development of knowledge discovery.

AI.tldr: DBench-Bio is a dynamic, automated benchmark for evaluating AI's biological knowledge discovery ability, addressing data contamination and outdated static benchmarks through monthly updates across 12 biomedical domains.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for evaluating AI knowledge discovery rely on static datasets, leading to data contamination (models having seen evaluation knowledge during training) and rapid obsolescence due to LLM release cycles. Current approaches fail to assess the ability to discover truly new knowledge.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: (1) Data acquisition of rigorous, authoritative paper abstracts; (2) QA extraction using LLMs to synthesize scientific hypothesis questions and corresponding discovery answers; (3) QA filter ensuring quality based on relevance, clarity, and centrality. This pipeline is instantiated to construct a monthly-updated benchmark covering 12 biomedical sub-domains.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations of state-of-the-art models reveal current limitations in discovering new knowledge. The benchmark provides the first dynamic, automatic framework for assessing new knowledge discovery capabilities.
AI.conclusion: DBench-Bio establishes a living, evolving resource for the AI research community to catalyze the development of knowledge discovery capabilities, addressing critical limitations of existing static evaluation approaches.

title: Discern Truth from Falsehood: Reducing Over-Refusal via Contrastive Refinement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) aligned for safety often suffer from over-refusal, the tendency to reject seemingly toxic or benign prompts by misclassifying them as toxic. This behavior undermines models' helpfulness and restricts usability in sensitive or nuanced contexts. While prior work has proposed mitigation strategies such as data augmentation and activation steering, these approaches often face a trade-off: reducing over-refusal typically degrades the model's ability to reject genuinely harmful content. We argue that this issue arises from the ambiguous influence of toxic and seemingly toxic prompts on the model's learning dynamics. To address it, we introduce a preceding alignment stage, DCR: Discernment via Contrastive Refinement. Both theoretically and empirically, we demonstrate that contrastive refinement improves an LLM's capacity to distinguish truly toxic prompts from superficially toxic ones. Evaluation across diverse benchmarks shows that our method effectively reduces over-refusal while preserving the safety benefits of alignment. Importantly, it achieves this with minimal degradation of general capabilities, offering a more principled and robust direction for safety alignment.

AI.tldr: DCR (Discernment via Contrastive Refinement) is a preceding alignment stage that reduces over-refusal in safety-aligned LLMs while preserving their ability to reject genuinely harmful content, addressing the trade-off between safety and helpfulness.
AI.motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs often suffer from over-refusal, rejecting both toxic and benign prompts, which undermines helpfulness and restricts usability in sensitive contexts. Existing mitigation strategies typically face a trade-off where reducing over-refusal degrades the model's ability to reject genuinely harmful content.
AI.method: Introduces DCR: Discernment via Contrastive Refinement, a preceding alignment stage that uses contrastive refinement to improve LLMs' capacity to distinguish truly toxic prompts from superficially toxic ones. The approach is supported by both theoretical and empirical analysis.
AI.result: Evaluation across diverse benchmarks shows DCR effectively reduces over-refusal while preserving safety benefits of alignment. The method achieves this with minimal degradation of general capabilities, offering improved performance compared to prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: DCR provides a more principled and robust direction for safety alignment by addressing the ambiguous influence of toxic and seemingly toxic prompts on learning dynamics, enabling better balance between safety and helpfulness in LLMs.

title: Controlling Chat Style in Language Models via Single-Direction Editing
summary: Controlling stylistic attributes in large language models (LLMs) remains challenging, with existing approaches relying on either prompt engineering or post-training alignment. This paper investigates this challenge through the lens of representation engineering, testing the hypothesis that distinct stylistic attributes - from emotional tone to linguistic structure - are encoded as linear directions in the model's activation space. We provide strong empirical evidence for this hypothesis across a wide range of styles and, based on this finding, present a lightweight, training-free method for precise style control. Our approach supports linear style composition, enhances safety by ablating undesirable behaviors, and, as confirmed by experiments on over a dozen models, achieves high style adherence while preserving core capabilities at minimal computational cost.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that stylistic attributes in LLMs are encoded as linear directions in activation space, enabling a lightweight, training-free method for precise style control through linear composition and ablation.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for controlling stylistic attributes in LLMs rely on either prompt engineering or post-training alignment, which can be inefficient or computationally expensive. The authors investigate whether stylistic attributes are encoded as linear directions in the model's activation space, which could enable more efficient control methods.
AI.method: The paper uses representation engineering to test the hypothesis that stylistic attributes are encoded as linear directions in activation space. Based on empirical evidence supporting this hypothesis, they develop a lightweight, training-free method for style control that supports linear style composition and can ablate undesirable behaviors by manipulating these linear directions.
AI.result: The approach provides strong empirical evidence that distinct stylistic attributes (emotional tone, linguistic structure, etc.) are indeed encoded as linear directions across a wide range of styles. Experiments on over a dozen models show the method achieves high style adherence while preserving core capabilities at minimal computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Stylistic attributes in LLMs are encoded as linear directions in activation space, enabling efficient, training-free control methods. This representation-based approach supports linear composition of styles, enhances safety through ablation of undesirable behaviors, and maintains model capabilities while providing precise style control.

title: IntPro: A Proxy Agent for Context-Aware Intent Understanding via Retrieval-conditioned Inference
