summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become integral to modern Human-AI collaboration workflows, where accurately understanding user intent serves as a crucial step for generating satisfactory responses. Context-aware intent understanding, which involves inferring user intentions from situational environments, is inherently challenging because it requires reasoning over both the immediate context and the user's underlying motivations that drive their behavior. Moreover, existing approaches often treat intent understanding as a static recognition task, overlooking users' accumulated intent patterns that could provide valuable references for more accurate and generalizable understanding. To address this gap, we propose IntPro, a proxy agent that learns to adapt to individual users via retrieval-conditioned intent inference. We design intent explanations that abstract how contextual signals connect to expressed intents, and store them in an individual intent history library for retrieval. We train IntPro through supervised fine-tuning on retrieval-conditioned trajectories and multi-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with tool-aware reward functions, enabling the agent to learn when to leverage historical intent patterns and when to infer directly. Experiments across three diverse scenarios (Highlight-Intent, MIntRec2.0, and Weibo Post-Sync) demonstrate that IntPro achieves strong intent understanding performance with effective context-aware reasoning capabilities across different scenarios and model types.

AI.tldr: IntPro is a proxy agent for context-aware intent understanding in LLM-based Human-AI collaboration that learns to adapt to individual users via retrieval-conditioned intent inference using historical intent patterns.
AI.motivation: Current approaches treat intent understanding as static recognition, overlooking users' accumulated intent patterns that could provide valuable references for more accurate and generalizable understanding. Context-aware intent understanding is challenging as it requires reasoning over both immediate context and underlying motivations.
AI.method: Proposes IntPro with intent explanations that abstract how contextual signals connect to expressed intents, stored in individual intent history libraries. Trained through supervised fine-tuning on retrieval-conditioned trajectories and multi-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with tool-aware reward functions to learn when to leverage historical patterns vs. infer directly.
AI.result: Experiments across three diverse scenarios (Highlight-Intent, MIntRec2.0, and Weibo Post-Sync) demonstrate strong intent understanding performance with effective context-aware reasoning capabilities across different scenarios and model types.
AI.conclusion: IntPro addresses the gap in existing static intent recognition approaches by enabling adaptive intent understanding through retrieval-conditioned inference and historical pattern utilization, improving context-aware reasoning in Human-AI collaboration workflows.

title: Controllable and explainable personality sliders for LLMs at inference time
summary: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with specific personas typically relies on expensive and monolithic Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) or RLHF. While effective, these methods require training distinct models for every target personality profile. Inference-time activation steering offers a parameter-efficient alternative, yet naive approaches fail to control multiple traits simultaneously due to destructive vector interference. In this work, we propose a modular framework for continuous, multi-dimensional personality control. Our key innovation is Sequential Adaptive Steering (SAS): a method that orthogonalizes steering vectors by training subsequent probes on the residual stream shifted by prior interventions. This approach transforms steering vectors into reusable primitives, allowing users to instantly synthesize complex, high-fidelity personality profiles by simply adjusting coefficients alpha. We validate our framework on the Big Five personality traits, demonstrating that it outperforms naive baselines in both goal adherence and coherence, enabling precise, holistic personality modulation without updating model parameters.

AI.tldr: SAS enables modular, multi-dimensional personality control in LLMs without parameter updates by orthogonalizing steering vectors to prevent interference.
AI.motivation: Current persona alignment methods require expensive per-profile training (SFT/RLHF) or suffer from destructive interference when controlling multiple traits simultaneously via activation steering.
AI.method: Sequential Adaptive Steering (SAS): orthogonalizes steering vectors by training subsequent probes on residual streams shifted by prior interventions, creating reusable primitives for personality synthesis.
AI.result: Outperforms naive baselines on Big Five personality traits in both goal adherence and coherence, enabling precise holistic personality modulation without parameter updates.
AI.conclusion: SAS provides a parameter-efficient framework for continuous, multi-dimensional personality control in LLMs, transforming steering vectors into reusable primitives for instant personality profile synthesis.

title: A benchmark for joint dialogue satisfaction, emotion recognition, and emotion state transition prediction
summary: User satisfaction is closely related to enterprises, as it not only directly reflects users' subjective evaluation of service quality or products, but also affects customer loyalty and long-term business revenue. Monitoring and understanding user emotions during interactions helps predict and improve satisfaction. However, relevant Chinese datasets are limited, and user emotions are dynamic; relying on single-turn dialogue cannot fully track emotional changes across multiple turns, which may affect satisfaction prediction. To address this, we constructed a multi-task, multi-label Chinese dialogue dataset that supports satisfaction recognition, as well as emotion recognition and emotional state transition prediction, providing new resources for studying emotion and satisfaction in dialogue systems.

AI.tldr: Constructed a multi-task, multi-label Chinese dialogue dataset for satisfaction recognition, emotion recognition, and emotional state transition prediction to address limited Chinese resources and dynamic emotion tracking challenges.
AI.motivation: User satisfaction is crucial for enterprises as it reflects service/product evaluation and affects customer loyalty and revenue. Current limitations include: 1) scarcity of relevant Chinese datasets, 2) dynamic nature of user emotions, and 3) inability of single-turn dialogue analysis to fully track emotional changes across multiple turns, which impacts satisfaction prediction accuracy.
AI.method: Constructed a multi-task, multi-label Chinese dialogue dataset that simultaneously supports three tasks: satisfaction recognition, emotion recognition, and emotional state transition prediction. The dataset enables comprehensive analysis of emotional dynamics across dialogue turns.
AI.result: Created a new Chinese dialogue dataset resource that facilitates the study of emotion and satisfaction in dialogue systems, addressing the gap in Chinese language resources and enabling better tracking of emotional changes across multiple dialogue turns.
AI.conclusion: The constructed multi-task, multi-label Chinese dialogue dataset provides valuable resources for improving satisfaction prediction by enabling comprehensive analysis of dynamic emotional changes across dialogue interactions, addressing limitations in existing Chinese language resources and single-turn analysis approaches.

title: StructLens: A Structural Lens for Language Models via Maximum Spanning Trees
summary: Language exhibits inherent structures, a property that explains both language acquisition and language change. Given this characteristic, we expect language models to manifest internal structures as well. While interpretability research has investigated the components of language models, existing approaches focus on local inter-token relationships within layers or modules (e.g., Multi-Head Attention), leaving global inter-layer relationships largely overlooked. To address this gap, we introduce StructLens, an analytical framework designed to reveal how internal structures relate holistically through their inter-token connection within a layer. StructLens constructs maximum spanning trees based on the semantic representations in residual streams, analogous to dependency parsing, and leverages the tree properties to quantify inter-layer distance (or similarity) from a structural perspective. Our findings demonstrate that StructLens yields an inter-layer similarity pattern that is distinctively different from conventional cosine similarity. Moreover, this structure-aware similarity proves to be beneficial for practical tasks, such as layer pruning, highlighting the effectiveness of structural analysis for understanding and optimizing language models. Our code is available at https://github.com/naist-nlp/structlens.

AI.tldr: StructLens is a framework that analyzes language model internal structures by constructing maximum spanning trees from residual stream representations to quantify inter-layer structural similarity, revealing patterns distinct from conventional cosine similarity and benefiting practical tasks like layer pruning.
AI.motivation: Language exhibits inherent structures that should be reflected in language models. While interpretability research has focused on local inter-token relationships within layers, global inter-layer structural relationships remain largely unexplored, creating a gap in understanding how language model components relate holistically.
AI.method: StructLens constructs maximum spanning trees based on semantic representations in residual streams, analogous to dependency parsing. It leverages tree properties to quantify inter-layer distance/similarity from a structural perspective, providing a framework to reveal how internal structures relate through inter-token connections within layers.
AI.result: StructLens yields inter-layer similarity patterns that are distinctively different from conventional cosine similarity. The structure-aware similarity proves beneficial for practical tasks such as layer pruning, demonstrating the effectiveness of structural analysis for understanding and optimizing language models.
AI.conclusion: Structural analysis of language models through frameworks like StructLens provides valuable insights into inter-layer relationships that differ from conventional similarity measures, offering practical benefits for model optimization and enhancing our understanding of how language structures manifest in neural models.

title: AutoHarness: improving LLM agents by automatically synthesizing a code harness
comment: agent harness, code synthesis, self-improvement, code-as-policy, text games
summary: Despite significant strides in language models in the last few years, when used as agents, such models often try to perform actions that are not just suboptimal for a given state, but are strictly prohibited by the external environment. For example, in the recent Kaggle GameArena chess competition, 78% of Gemini-2.5-Flash losses were attributed to illegal moves. Often people manually write "harnesses" around LLMs to prevent such failures. In this paper, we demonstrate that Gemini-2.5-Flash can automatically synthesize such a code harness, using a small number of rounds of iterative code refinement given feedback from the (game) environment. The resulting harness prevents all illegal moves in 145 different TextArena games (both 1-player and 2-player), enabling the smaller Gemini-2.5-Flash model to outperform larger models, such as Gemini-2.5-Pro. Pushing our technique to the limit, we can get Gemini-2.5-Flash to generate the entire policy in code, thus eliminating the need to use the LLM at decision making time. The resulting code-policy receives a higher average reward than Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5.2-High on 16 TextArena 1-player games. Our results show that using a smaller model to synthesize a custom code harness (or entire policy) can outperform a much larger model, while also being more cost effective.

AI.tldr: Gemini-2.5-Flash can automatically synthesize code harnesses to prevent illegal moves in game environments, enabling it to outperform larger models like Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5.2-High through iterative code refinement.
AI.motivation: Language models used as agents often make prohibited moves in external environments (e.g., 78% of Gemini-2.5-Flash losses in chess were illegal moves), requiring manual code harnesses to prevent such failures.
AI.method: Gemini-2.5-Flash automatically synthesizes code harnesses through iterative code refinement using feedback from game environments, preventing illegal moves in 145 TextArena games. The approach can generate entire policies in code, eliminating LLM use at decision time.
AI.result: The synthesized harness prevents all illegal moves, enabling Gemini-2.5-Flash to outperform larger models. Code-policies achieve higher average reward than Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5.2-High on 16 TextArena 1-player games.
AI.conclusion: Smaller models can synthesize custom code harnesses or entire policies that outperform larger models while being more cost-effective, demonstrating the value of automated code generation for reliable agent behavior.

title: Certainty robustness: Evaluating LLM stability under self-challenging prompts
comment: 20 pages, 7 tables Benchmark and evaluation study of large language models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often present answers with high apparent confidence despite lacking an explicit mechanism for reasoning about certainty or truth. While existing benchmarks primarily evaluate single-turn accuracy, truthfulness or confidence calibration, they do not capture how models behave when their responses are challenged in interactive settings. We introduce the Certainty Robustness Benchmark, a two-turn evaluation framework that measures how LLMs balance stability and adaptability under self-challenging prompts such as uncertainty ("Are you sure?") and explicit contradiction ("You are wrong!"), alongside numeric confidence elicitation. Using 200 reasoning and mathematics questions from LiveBench, we evaluate four state-of-the-art LLMs and distinguish between justified self-corrections and unjustified answer changes. Our results reveal substantial differences in interactive reliability that are not explained by baseline accuracy alone: some models abandon correct answers under conversational pressure, while others demonstrate strong resistance to challenge and better alignment between confidence and correctness. These findings identify certainty robustness as a distinct and critical dimension of LLM evaluation, with important implications for alignment, trustworthiness and real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: The Certainty Robustness Benchmark evaluates how LLMs handle conversational challenges to their answers, revealing that baseline accuracy alone doesn't predict how models respond to uncertainty prompts and contradictions.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate single-turn accuracy, truthfulness, or confidence calibration but fail to capture how LLMs behave when their responses are challenged in interactive settings, which is crucial for real-world deployment and trustworthiness.
AI.method: A two-turn evaluation framework using 200 reasoning and mathematics questions from LiveBench, testing LLMs with self-challenging prompts like "Are you sure?" and "You are wrong!", alongside numeric confidence elicitation, distinguishing between justified self-corrections and unjustified answer changes.
AI.result: Substantial differences in interactive reliability not explained by baseline accuracy alone: some models abandon correct answers under conversational pressure, while others demonstrate strong resistance to challenge and better alignment between confidence and correctness.
AI.conclusion: Certainty robustness is a distinct and critical dimension of LLM evaluation with important implications for alignment, trustworthiness, and real-world deployment, highlighting the need for interactive evaluation beyond single-turn metrics.

title: PulseLM: A Foundation Dataset and Benchmark for PPG-Text Learning
summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a widely used non-invasive sensing modality for continuous cardiovascular and physiological monitoring across clinical, laboratory, and wearable settings. While existing PPG datasets support a broad range of downstream tasks, they typically provide supervision in the form of numerical measurements or task-specific labels, limiting their suitability for language-based physiological reasoning and multimodal foundation models. In this work, we introduce PulseLM, a large-scale PPG-text dataset designed to bridge raw PPG waveforms and natural language through a unified, closed-ended question answering (QA) formulation. PulseLM aggregates PPG recordings from fifteen publicly available sources and harmonizes heterogeneous annotations into twelve common physiologically QA tasks. The dataset comprises 1.31 million standardized 10-second PPG segments, associated with 3.15 million question-answer pairs. We further define reproducible preprocessing, supervision, and evaluation protocols and establish baseline benchmarks using multimodal PPG-aware large language models. PulseLM provides a standardized foundation for studying multimodal physiological reasoning, cross-dataset generalization, and scalable benchmarking of PPG-based language models. The data and code can be found publicly available at: https://github.com/manhph2211/PulseLM.

AI.tldr: PulseLM is a large-scale PPG-text dataset with 1.31M PPG segments and 3.15M QA pairs, designed to bridge raw PPG waveforms with natural language for multimodal physiological reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing PPG datasets provide numerical measurements or task-specific labels, limiting their suitability for language-based physiological reasoning and multimodal foundation models. There's a need to bridge raw PPG waveforms with natural language.
AI.method: Aggregated PPG recordings from 15 public sources and harmonized heterogeneous annotations into 12 common physiological QA tasks using a closed-ended question answering formulation. Created standardized preprocessing, supervision, and evaluation protocols.
AI.result: Created PulseLM dataset with 1.31 million standardized 10-second PPG segments associated with 3.15 million question-answer pairs. Established baseline benchmarks using multimodal PPG-aware large language models.
AI.conclusion: PulseLM provides a standardized foundation for studying multimodal physiological reasoning, cross-dataset generalization, and scalable benchmarking of PPG-based language models, with publicly available data and code.

title: Fragile Thoughts: How Large Language Models Handle Chain-of-Thought Perturbations
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a foundational technique for eliciting reasoning from Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the robustness of this approach to corruptions in intermediate reasoning steps remains poorly understood. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation of LLM robustness to a structured taxonomy of 5 CoT perturbation types: \textit{MathError, UnitConversion, Sycophancy, SkippedSteps,} and \textit{ExtraSteps}. We evaluate 13 models spanning three orders of magnitude in parameter count (3B to 1.5T\footnote{Assumed parameter count of closed models}), testing their ability to complete mathematical reasoning tasks despite perturbations injected at different points in the reasoning chain. Our key findings reveal heterogeneous vulnerability patterns: MathError perturbations produce the most severe degradation in small models (50-60\% accuracy loss) but show strong scaling benefits; UnitConversion remains challenging across all scales (20-30\% loss even for largest models); ExtraSteps incur minimal accuracy degradation (0-6\%) regardless of scale; Sycophancy produces modest effects (7\% loss for small models); and SkippedSteps cause intermediate damage (15\% loss). Scaling relationships follow power-law patterns, with model size serving as a protective factor against some perturbations but offering limited defense against dimensional reasoning tasks. These findings have direct implications for deploying LLMs in multi-stage reasoning pipelines and underscore the necessity of task-specific robustness assessments and mitigation strategies. The code and results are available \href{https://github.com/Mystic-Slice/CoTPerturbation}{here}.

AI.tldr: LLM robustness to CoT perturbations varies by type: MathError hits small models hardest but scales well, UnitConversion remains challenging at all scales, ExtraSteps cause minimal harm, Sycophancy modest effects, SkippedSteps intermediate damage.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought prompting is widely used but its robustness to corruptions in intermediate reasoning steps is poorly understood, creating risks for deploying LLMs in multi-stage reasoning pipelines.
AI.method: Comprehensive empirical evaluation of 13 LLMs (3B to 1.5T parameters) on mathematical reasoning tasks with 5 structured CoT perturbation types: MathError, UnitConversion, Sycophancy, SkippedSteps, and ExtraSteps injected at different points in reasoning chains.
AI.result: Heterogeneous vulnerability patterns: MathError causes 50-60% accuracy loss in small models but shows strong scaling benefits; UnitConversion remains challenging (20-30% loss even for largest models); ExtraSteps minimal degradation (0-6%); Sycophancy modest (7% loss for small models); SkippedSteps intermediate (15% loss). Scaling follows power-law patterns with model size as protective factor for some perturbations but limited defense against dimensional reasoning.
AI.conclusion: LLM robustness to CoT perturbations varies significantly by perturbation type, with scaling benefits not uniform across all reasoning failures. Findings highlight need for task-specific robustness assessments and mitigation strategies for reliable deployment in multi-stage reasoning pipelines.

title: Training-free Dropout Sampling for Semantic Token Acceptance in Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by proposing tokens with a lightweight draft model and selectively accepting them using a target model. This work introduces DropMatch, a novel approach that matches draft tokens to the predictive distribution of the target model via Monte Carlo dropout applied exclusively to the LM head, enabling sampling-based acceptance decisions. By generating multiple decoding paths, our method forms an empirical token distribution against which draft tokens are evaluated for consistency. This acceptance mechanism enables the model to adaptively control the size of decoding paths under an appropriate dropout probability, preventing substantial distortion of the target model predictive distribution. The proposed method operates in a training-free, data-free, and calibration-free manner, requires no architectural modification to pretrained models, and can be orthogonally integrated with a wide range of existing speculative decoding and inference acceleration techniques. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach increases acceptance length while maintaining competitive task performance, yielding inference speedups ranging from 1.09x to 1.33x over the standard baseline, and up to an additional 1.09x speedup when applied on top of EAGLE3.

AI.tldr: DropMatch improves speculative decoding by using Monte Carlo dropout on the LM head to generate multiple decoding paths, enabling sampling-based acceptance decisions that increase token acceptance rates without model modifications.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference but faces challenges in effectively matching draft tokens to the target model's predictive distribution, limiting acceptance rates and speedup potential.
AI.method: Apply Monte Carlo dropout exclusively to the LM head to generate multiple decoding paths, forming an empirical token distribution for evaluating draft token consistency. This enables adaptive control of decoding path size under appropriate dropout probabilities while preventing distortion of the target model's predictive distribution.
AI.result: Increases acceptance length while maintaining competitive task performance, achieving inference speedups of 1.09x to 1.33x over standard baselines, with up to additional 1.09x speedup when combined with EAGLE3.
AI.conclusion: DropMatch provides a training-free, data-free, calibration-free approach that requires no architectural modifications and can be orthogonally integrated with existing speculative decoding techniques, offering practical inference acceleration.

title: The CompMath-MCQ Dataset: Are LLMs Ready for Higher-Level Math?
summary: The evaluation of Large Language Models (LLMs) on mathematical reasoning has largely focused on elementary problems, competition-style questions, or formal theorem proving, leaving graduate-level and computational mathematics relatively underexplored. We introduce CompMath-MCQ, a new benchmark dataset for assessing LLMs on advanced mathematical reasoning in a multiple-choice setting. The dataset consists of 1{,}500 originally authored questions by professors of graduate-level courses, covering topics including Linear Algebra, Numerical Optimization, Vector Calculus, Probability, and Python-based scientific computing. Three option choices are provided for each question, with exactly one of them being correct. To ensure the absence of data leakage, all questions are newly created and not sourced from existing materials. The validity of questions is verified through a procedure based on cross-LLM disagreement, followed by manual expert review. By adopting a multiple-choice format, our dataset enables objective, reproducible, and bias-free evaluation through lm_eval library. Baseline results with state-of-the-art LLMs indicate that advanced computational mathematical reasoning remains a significant challenge. We release CompMath-MCQ at the following link: https://github.com/biancaraimondi/CompMath-MCQ.git

AI.tldr: CompMath-MCQ is a new benchmark dataset of 1,500 originally authored graduate-level mathematics multiple-choice questions for evaluating LLMs on advanced computational mathematics reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation on mathematical reasoning focuses on elementary problems, competition-style questions, or formal theorem proving, leaving graduate-level and computational mathematics relatively underexplored.
AI.method: Created 1,500 originally authored multiple-choice questions by professors of graduate-level courses covering Linear Algebra, Numerical Optimization, Vector Calculus, Probability, and Python-based scientific computing. Questions have three options with exactly one correct answer. Used cross-LLM disagreement analysis for validation followed by manual expert review to ensure no data leakage.
AI.result: Baseline results with state-of-the-art LLMs indicate that advanced computational mathematical reasoning remains a significant challenge for current models.
AI.conclusion: CompMath-MCQ enables objective, reproducible, and bias-free evaluation of LLMs on advanced mathematical reasoning through the lm_eval library, addressing a gap in current benchmarking approaches.

title: Compressed Sensing for Capability Localization in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a wide range of capabilities, including mathematical reasoning, code generation, and linguistic behaviors. We show that many capabilities are highly localized to small subsets of attention heads within Transformer architectures. Zeroing out as few as five task-specific heads can degrade performance by up to $65\%$ on standard benchmarks measuring the capability of interest, while largely preserving performance on unrelated tasks. We introduce a compressed sensing based method that exploits the sparsity of these heads to identify them via strategic knockouts and a small number of model evaluations. We validate these findings across Llama and Qwen models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters and a diverse set of capabilities including mathematical abilities and code generation, revealing a modular organization in which specialized capabilities are implemented by sparse, functionally distinct components. Overall, our results suggest that capability localization is a general organizational principle of Transformer language models, with implications for interpretability, model editing, and AI safety. Code is released at https://github.com/locuslab/llm-components.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that specific capabilities in LLMs are localized to small subsets of attention heads, which can be identified and manipulated with minimal impact on unrelated tasks.
AI.motivation: To understand the internal organization of capabilities in large language models and demonstrate that specific abilities are highly localized to sparse subsets of attention heads rather than being distributed throughout the network.
AI.method: Uses a compressed sensing approach with strategic knockouts to identify task-specific attention heads, requiring only a small number of model evaluations. Validates across Llama and Qwen models (1B-8B parameters) on diverse capabilities including mathematical reasoning and code generation.
AI.result: Zeroing out just 5 task-specific heads can degrade performance by up to 65% on targeted capabilities while preserving performance on unrelated tasks. The method successfully identifies sparse, functionally distinct components responsible for specific capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Capability localization is a general organizational principle in Transformer language models, with important implications for interpretability, model editing, and AI safety. The modular organization suggests specialized capabilities are implemented by sparse components.

title: Prompt-Dependent Ranking of Large Language Models with Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Rankings derived from pairwise comparisons are central to many economic and computational systems. In the context of large language models (LLMs), rankings are typically constructed from human preference data and presented as leaderboards that guide deployment decisions. However, existing approaches rely on point estimates, implicitly treating rankings as fixed objects despite substantial estimation noise and context-dependent performance variation. Acting on such rankings can lead to misallocation and welfare loss when apparent differences are not statistically meaningful. We study prompt-dependent ranking inference under pairwise human preferences and develop a framework for decision-safe rankings with statistically valid uncertainty guarantees. We model preferences using a contextual Bradley-Terry-Luce model in which the latent utility of each model depends on the input prompt. Rather than targeting point estimates of utilities, we directly conduct inference on induced rankings, constructing confidence sets based on simultaneous confidence intervals for pairwise utility differences. This approach yields statistically valid marginal and simultaneous confidence sets for prompt-specific ranks. Our framework connects recent advances in rank inference to contextual preference learning and provides tools for robust ranking-based decision-making. Empirically, using large-scale human preference data from LLM evaluations, we show that rankings vary substantially across prompt characteristics and that many apparent rank differences are not statistically distinguishable. We further demonstrate how uncertainty-aware rankings identify dominance only when supported by the data and otherwise return partial orders.

AI.tldr: A framework for statistically valid ranking inference in LLM evaluations using contextual preference models, addressing uncertainty in pairwise comparisons to prevent misallocation based on noisy point estimates.
AI.motivation: Current LLM ranking systems rely on point estimates that ignore substantial estimation noise and context-dependent performance variation, leading to potential misallocation and welfare loss when apparent rank differences are not statistically meaningful.
AI.method: Develops a contextual Bradley-Terry-Luce model where latent utility depends on input prompts, then constructs confidence sets using simultaneous confidence intervals for pairwise utility differences to conduct inference directly on induced rankings rather than targeting point estimates.
AI.result: Empirical analysis using large-scale human preference data shows rankings vary substantially across prompt characteristics, with many apparent rank differences not statistically distinguishable; uncertainty-aware rankings identify dominance only when supported by data and otherwise return partial orders.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides statistically valid marginal and simultaneous confidence sets for prompt-specific ranks, connecting rank inference advances to contextual preference learning and enabling robust ranking-based decision-making with uncertainty guarantees.

title: Tracing Pharmacological Knowledge In Large Language Models
comment: Accepted, Learning Meaningful Representations of Life (LMRL) Workshop @ ICLR 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong empirical performance across pharmacology and drug discovery tasks, yet the internal mechanisms by which they encode pharmacological knowledge remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate how drug-group semantics are represented and retrieved within Llama-based biomedical language models using causal and probing-based interpretability methods. We apply activation patching to localize where drug-group information is stored across model layers and token positions, and complement this analysis with linear probes trained on token-level and sum-pooled activations. Our results demonstrate that early layers play a key role in encoding drug-group knowledge, with the strongest causal effects arising from intermediate tokens within the drug-group span rather than the final drug-group token. Linear probing further reveals that pharmacological semantics are distributed across tokens and are already present in the embedding space, with token-level probes performing near chance while sum-pooled representations achieve maximal accuracy. Together, these findings suggest that drug-group semantics in LLMs are not localized to single tokens but instead arise from distributed representations. This study provides the first systematic mechanistic analysis of pharmacological knowledge in LLMs, offering insights into how biomedical semantics are encoded in large language models.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how drug-group semantics are represented in Llama-based biomedical LLMs using causal and probing interpretability methods, finding that pharmacological knowledge is distributed across tokens rather than localized to single tokens.
AI.motivation: While LLMs show strong performance in pharmacology and drug discovery tasks, the internal mechanisms by which they encode pharmacological knowledge remain poorly understood. The authors aim to systematically analyze how drug-group semantics are represented and retrieved within biomedical language models.
AI.method: The study uses causal and probing-based interpretability methods on Llama-based biomedical language models. Specifically, they apply activation patching to localize where drug-group information is stored across model layers and token positions, and complement this with linear probes trained on both token-level and sum-pooled activations.
AI.result: Early layers play a key role in encoding drug-group knowledge, with strongest causal effects from intermediate tokens within drug-group spans rather than final tokens. Linear probing shows pharmacological semantics are distributed across tokens and already present in embedding space - token-level probes perform near chance while sum-pooled representations achieve maximal accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Drug-group semantics in LLMs are not localized to single tokens but instead arise from distributed representations. This study provides the first systematic mechanistic analysis of pharmacological knowledge in LLMs, offering insights into how biomedical semantics are encoded in large language models.

title: Farther the Shift, Sparser the Representation: Analyzing OOD Mechanisms in LLMs
summary: In this work, we investigate how Large Language Models (LLMs) adapt their internal representations when encountering inputs of increasing difficulty, quantified as the degree of out-of-distribution (OOD) shift. We reveal a consistent and quantifiable phenomenon: as task difficulty increases, whether through harder reasoning questions, longer contexts, or adding answer choices, the last hidden states of LLMs become substantially sparser. In short, \textbf{\textit{the farther the shift, the sparser the representations}}. This sparsity--difficulty relation is observable across diverse models and domains, suggesting that language models respond to unfamiliar or complex inputs by concentrating computation into specialized subspaces in the last hidden state. Through a series of controlled analyses with a learning dynamic explanation, we demonstrate that this sparsity is not incidental but an adaptive mechanism for stabilizing reasoning under OOD. Leveraging this insight, we design \textit{Sparsity-Guided Curriculum In-Context Learning (SG-ICL)}, a strategy that explicitly uses representation sparsity to schedule few-shot demonstrations, leading to considerable performance enhancements. Our study provides new mechanistic insights into how LLMs internalize OOD challenges. The source code is available at the URL: https://github.com/MingyuJ666/sparsityLLM.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit sparser last hidden state representations as task difficulty increases due to out-of-distribution (OOD) shift, and this sparsity-difficulty relation enables improved in-context learning via sparsity-guided curriculum scheduling.
AI.motivation: To understand how LLMs adapt their internal representations when facing increasingly difficult inputs (quantified as OOD shift), and to investigate whether observed sparsity patterns represent an adaptive mechanism for handling unfamiliar or complex inputs.
AI.method: Analyze sparsity of last hidden states across diverse models and domains as task difficulty increases (harder reasoning questions, longer contexts, more answer choices). Conduct controlled analyses with learning dynamic explanations to determine if sparsity is adaptive. Design Sparsity-Guided Curriculum In-Context Learning (SG-ICL) that uses representation sparsity to schedule few-shot demonstrations.
AI.result: Reveal consistent sparsity-difficulty relation: "the farther the shift, the sparser the representations." Show this phenomenon is observable across diverse models and domains. Demonstrate sparsity is not incidental but an adaptive mechanism for stabilizing reasoning under OOD. SG-ICL leads to considerable performance enhancements in in-context learning.
AI.conclusion: LLMs respond to unfamiliar or complex inputs by concentrating computation into specialized subspaces in the last hidden state, providing new mechanistic insights into how LLMs internalize OOD challenges. The sparsity-difficulty relation enables practical improvements in in-context learning through sparsity-guided curriculum scheduling.

title: Raising Bars, Not Parameters: LilMoo Compact Language Model for Hindi
summary: The dominance of large multilingual foundation models has widened linguistic inequalities in Natural Language Processing (NLP), often leaving low-resource languages underrepresented. This paper introduces LilMoo, a 0.6-billion-parameter Hindi language model trained entirely from scratch to address this gap. Unlike prior Hindi models that rely on continual pretraining from opaque multilingual foundations, LilMoo is developed through a fully transparent and reproducible pipeline optimized for limited compute environments. We construct a high-quality Hindi corpus (GigaLekh) filtered through both heuristic and learned (LLM-as-a-judge) methods, complemented by bilingual augmentation with curated English data. Using this dataset, we explore various training recipes for small-scale language models. Across comprehensive evaluation suites, LilMoo consistently outperforms comparably sized multilingual baselines such as Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen3-0.6B, demonstrating that well-designed language-specific pretraining can rival large multilingual models at the sub-billion-parameter range.

AI.tldr: LilMoo is a 0.6B parameter Hindi language model trained from scratch to address linguistic inequalities, outperforming comparable multilingual models through transparent development and high-quality Hindi data curation.
AI.motivation: Large multilingual foundation models have created linguistic inequalities in NLP, leaving low-resource languages like Hindi underrepresented. Existing Hindi models rely on opaque multilingual foundations through continual pretraining, lacking transparency and reproducibility.
AI.method: Developed LilMoo from scratch using a transparent pipeline optimized for limited compute. Constructed high-quality Hindi corpus (GigaLekh) filtered via heuristic and LLM-as-a-judge methods, with bilingual English augmentation. Explored various training recipes for small-scale language models.
AI.result: LilMoo consistently outperforms comparably sized multilingual baselines (Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen3-0.6B) across comprehensive evaluation suites, demonstrating that well-designed language-specific pretraining can rival large multilingual models at sub-billion parameter scale.
AI.conclusion: Language-specific models like LilMoo offer a viable alternative to large multilingual foundations for low-resource languages, providing better performance with transparency and reproducibility while requiring fewer computational resources.

title: A theoretical model of dynamical grammatical gender shifting based on set-valued set function
summary: This study investigates the diverse characteristics of nouns, focusing on both semantic (e.g., countable/uncountable) and morphosyntactic (e.g., masculine/feminine) distinctions. We explore inter-word variations for gender markers in noun morphology. Grammatical gender shift is a widespread phenomenon in languages around the world. The aim is to uncover through a formal model the underlying patterns governing the variation of lexemes. To this end, we propose a new computational component dedicated to pairing items with morphological templates (e.g., the result of a generated item-template pair: (funas, $\{N, +SG, -PL, -M, +F, -COL, +SING\}$), with its spell-out form: $ð$a-funast 'cow'). This process is formally represented by the Template-Based and Modular Cognitive model. This proposed model, defined by a set-valued set function $h : \mathscr{P}(M) \rightarrow \mathscr{P}(M)$, predicts the nonlinear dynamic mapping of lexical items onto morphological templates. By applying this formalism, we present a unified framework for understanding the complexities of morphological markings across languages. Through empirical observations, we demonstrate how these shifts, as well as non-gender shifts, arise during lexical changes, especially in Riffian. Our model posits that these variant markings emerge due to template shifts occurring during word and meaning's formation. By formally demonstrating that conversion is applicable to noun-to-noun derivation, we challenge and broaden the conventional view of word formation. This mathematical model not only contributes to a deeper understanding of morphosyntactic variation but also offers potential applications in other fields requiring precise modelling of linguistic patterns.

AI.tldr: A computational model for analyzing noun variation patterns, focusing on semantic and morphosyntactic distinctions like gender and countability, using template-based mapping to explain morphological shifts in languages.
AI.motivation: To understand the complex patterns of noun variation across languages, particularly focusing on grammatical gender shifts and other morphosyntactic distinctions that are widespread but not well-formalized in existing linguistic models.
AI.method: Proposes a Template-Based and Modular Cognitive model using a set-valued set function h: ℘(M) → ℘(M) to map lexical items onto morphological templates, with empirical validation through Riffian language data and demonstration of noun-to-noun derivation.
AI.result: The model successfully explains gender shifts and non-gender morphological variations as template shifts during word formation, provides a unified framework for cross-linguistic morphological analysis, and demonstrates conversion applicability to noun-to-noun derivation.
AI.conclusion: The mathematical formalism offers a deeper understanding of morphosyntactic variation, challenges traditional word formation views, and has potential applications beyond linguistics for modeling complex pattern systems.

title: SafeCRS: Personalized Safety Alignment for LLM-Based Conversational Recommender Systems
summary: Current LLM-based conversational recommender systems (CRS) primarily optimize recommendation accuracy and user satisfaction. We identify an underexplored vulnerability in which recommendation outputs may negatively impact users by violating personalized safety constraints, when individualized safety sensitivities -- such as trauma triggers, self-harm history, or phobias -- are implicitly inferred from the conversation but not respected during recommendation. We formalize this challenge as personalized CRS safety and introduce SafeRec, a new benchmark dataset designed to systematically evaluate safety risks in LLM-based CRS under user-specific constraints. To further address this problem, we propose SafeCRS, a safety-aware training framework that integrates Safe Supervised Fine-Tuning (Safe-SFT) with Safe Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (Safe-GDPO) to jointly optimize recommendation quality and personalized safety alignment. Extensive experiments on SafeRec demonstrate that SafeCRS reduces safety violation rates by up to 96.5% relative to the strongest recommendation-quality baseline while maintaining competitive recommendation quality. Warning: This paper contains potentially harmful and offensive content.

AI.tldr: SafeCRS framework addresses personalized safety risks in LLM-based conversational recommender systems by integrating safety-aware training to respect user-specific constraints while maintaining recommendation quality.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based conversational recommender systems focus on accuracy and satisfaction but neglect personalized safety vulnerabilities where recommendations may violate individual constraints like trauma triggers, self-harm history, or phobias inferred from conversations.
AI.method: Proposes SafeCRS framework combining Safe Supervised Fine-Tuning (Safe-SFT) with Safe Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization (Safe-GDPO) to jointly optimize recommendation quality and personalized safety alignment.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on SafeRec benchmark show SafeCRS reduces safety violation rates by up to 96.5% relative to strongest recommendation-quality baselines while maintaining competitive recommendation quality.
AI.conclusion: The work formalizes personalized CRS safety as a critical challenge, introduces SafeRec benchmark for systematic evaluation, and demonstrates SafeCRS effectively addresses safety risks without compromising recommendation performance.

title: RAG-X: Systematic Diagnosis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Question Answering
summary: Automated question-answering (QA) systems increasingly rely on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground large language models (LLMs) in authoritative medical knowledge, ensuring clinical accuracy and patient safety in Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications for healthcare. Despite progress in RAG evaluation, current benchmarks focus only on simple multiple-choice QA tasks and employ metrics that poorly capture the semantic precision required for complex QA tasks. These approaches fail to diagnose whether an error stems from faulty retrieval or flawed generation, limiting developers from performing targeted improvement. To address this gap, we propose RAG-X, a diagnostic framework that evaluates the retriever and generator independently across a triad of QA tasks: information extraction, short-answer generation, and multiple-choice question (MCQ) answering. RAG-X introduces Context Utilization Efficiency (CUE) metrics to disaggregate system success into interpretable quadrants, isolating verified grounding from deceptive accuracy. Our experiments reveal an ``Accuracy Fallacy", where a 14\% gap separates perceived system success from evidence-based grounding. By surfacing hidden failure modes, RAG-X offers the diagnostic transparency needed for safe and verifiable clinical RAG systems.

AI.tldr: RAG-X is a diagnostic framework that independently evaluates retriever and generator components in medical QA systems, revealing a 14% "Accuracy Fallacy" gap between perceived success and evidence-based grounding.
AI.motivation: Current RAG evaluation benchmarks focus only on simple multiple-choice QA tasks with metrics that poorly capture semantic precision for complex QA. They fail to diagnose whether errors stem from faulty retrieval or flawed generation, limiting targeted improvements in clinical RAG systems where accuracy and patient safety are critical.
AI.method: Proposes RAG-X framework that evaluates retriever and generator independently across three QA tasks: information extraction, short-answer generation, and multiple-choice question answering. Introduces Context Utilization Efficiency (CUE) metrics to disaggregate system success into interpretable quadrants, isolating verified grounding from deceptive accuracy.
AI.result: Experiments reveal an "Accuracy Fallacy" where a 14% gap separates perceived system success from evidence-based grounding. The framework surfaces hidden failure modes that traditional evaluation approaches miss.
AI.conclusion: RAG-X provides the diagnostic transparency needed for safe and verifiable clinical RAG systems by enabling targeted improvements through independent evaluation of retriever and generator components, addressing critical gaps in current RAG evaluation methodologies for healthcare applications.

title: Tucano 2 Cool: Better Open Source LLMs for Portuguese
summary: We present Tucano 2, a fully open suite of large language models (LLMs) with 0.5-3.7 billion parameters, designed to address certain gaps in open-source development for Portuguese LLMs. Following our previous works, we now extend our dataset, GigaVerbo-v2, to a new degree of quality and scale, while also introducing a new synthetic dataset, GigaVerbo-v2 Synth, aimed at filling missing gaps in GigaVerbo-v2, and two post-training datasets, GigaVerbo-v2 SFT and GigaVerbo-v2 Preferences, that allow Portuguese LLMs to be trained in domains like retrieval augmented generation, coding, tool use, chain-of-thought reasoning, and many other domains of interest. Through extensive ablation studies, we design both pretraining and continual pretraining recipes for the Tucano 2 suite (Base, Instruct, and Think), which achieve state-of-the-art performance on several Portuguese-language modeling benchmarks. We also extend and refine the evaluation harness introduced in our earlier work, yielding a comprehensive evaluation suite that provides strong signals across different pretraining, continual pretraining, and post-training regimes. All artifacts associated with Tucano 2 are openly released, including training recipes, logs, and source code, ensuring that our work is reproducible, accessible, and extendable by the broader Portuguese NLP community.

AI.tldr: Tucano 2 is an open-source suite of Portuguese LLMs (0.5-3.7B parameters) with enhanced datasets and training recipes that achieve SOTA performance on Portuguese benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address gaps in open-source development for Portuguese LLMs by creating comprehensive, high-quality models and datasets for the Portuguese NLP community.
AI.method: Extends GigaVerbo-v2 dataset with synthetic data (GigaVerbo-v2 Synth) and post-training datasets (SFT and Preferences). Develops pretraining and continual pretraining recipes for three model variants (Base, Instruct, Think) with comprehensive evaluation suite.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on several Portuguese-language modeling benchmarks. All artifacts (training recipes, logs, source code) are openly released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: Tucano 2 provides a comprehensive, open-source solution for Portuguese LLMs with enhanced datasets, training methodologies, and evaluation tools that benefit the broader Portuguese NLP community.

title: ByteFlow: Language Modeling through Adaptive Byte Compression without a Tokenizer
summary: Modern language models still rely on fixed, pre-defined subword tokenizations. Once a tokenizer is trained, the LM can only operate at this fixed level of granularity, which often leads to brittle and counterintuitive behaviors even in otherwise strong reasoning models. We introduce \textbf{ByteFlow Net}, a new hierarchical architecture that removes tokenizers entirely and instead enables models to learn their own segmentation of raw byte streams into semantically meaningful units. ByteFlow Net performs compression-driven segmentation based on the coding rate of latent representations, yielding adaptive boundaries \emph{while preserving a static computation graph via Top-$K$ selection}. Unlike prior self-tokenizing methods that depend on brittle heuristics with human-designed inductive biases, ByteFlow Net adapts its internal representation granularity to the input itself. Experiments demonstrate that this compression-based chunking strategy yields substantial performance gains, with ByteFlow Net outperforming both BPE-based Transformers and previous byte-level architectures. These results suggest that end-to-end, tokenizer-free modeling is not only feasible but also more effective, opening a path toward more adaptive and information-grounded language models.

AI.tldr: ByteFlow Net is a hierarchical architecture that eliminates fixed tokenizers by learning adaptive segmentation of raw byte streams using compression-driven chunking based on coding rate, outperforming traditional BPE-based Transformers.
AI.motivation: Fixed subword tokenizations in modern language models lead to brittle and counterintuitive behaviors, limiting model adaptability and requiring pre-defined granularity that may not match semantic boundaries.
AI.method: ByteFlow Net uses compression-driven segmentation based on coding rate of latent representations, with adaptive boundaries maintained through Top-K selection to preserve static computation graphs, enabling models to learn their own segmentation of raw byte streams.
AI.result: ByteFlow Net outperforms both BPE-based Transformers and previous byte-level architectures, demonstrating substantial performance gains from compression-based chunking strategy.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end, tokenizer-free modeling is not only feasible but more effective, opening a path toward more adaptive and information-grounded language models that can learn appropriate segmentation granularity from data.

title: Belief-Sim: Towards Belief-Driven Simulation of Demographic Misinformation Susceptibility
summary: Misinformation is a growing societal threat, and susceptibility to misinformative claims varies across demographic groups due to differences in underlying beliefs. As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behaviors, we investigate whether they can simulate demographic misinformation susceptibility, treating beliefs as a primary driving factor. We introduce BeliefSim, a simulation framework that constructs demographic belief profiles using psychology-informed taxonomies and survey priors. We study prompt-based conditioning and post-training adaptation, and conduct a multi-fold evaluation using: (i) susceptibility accuracy and (ii) counterfactual demographic sensitivity. Across both datasets and modeling strategies, we show that beliefs provide a strong prior for simulating misinformation susceptibility, with accuracy up to 92%.

AI.tldr: BeliefSim framework uses demographic belief profiles to simulate misinformation susceptibility in LLMs, achieving up to 92% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Misinformation susceptibility varies across demographic groups due to differences in underlying beliefs, and there's a need to investigate whether LLMs can accurately simulate this demographic variation for research purposes.
AI.method: Introduces BeliefSim framework that constructs demographic belief profiles using psychology-informed taxonomies and survey priors. Studies prompt-based conditioning and post-training adaptation, with evaluation using susceptibility accuracy and counterfactual demographic sensitivity metrics.
AI.result: Across datasets and modeling strategies, beliefs provide a strong prior for simulating misinformation susceptibility, achieving accuracy up to 92%.
AI.conclusion: Belief profiles serve as effective priors for simulating demographic misinformation susceptibility in LLMs, enabling more accurate behavioral simulations for misinformation research.

title: A Neural Topic Method Using a Large-Language-Model-in-the-Loop for Business Research
summary: The growing use of unstructured text in business research makes topic modeling a central tool for constructing explanatory variables from reviews, social media, and open-ended survey responses, yet existing approaches function poorly as measurement instruments. Prior work shows that textual content predicts outcomes such as sales, satisfaction, and firm performance, but probabilistic models often generate conceptually diffuse topics, neural topic models are difficult to interpret in theory-driven settings, and large language model approaches lack standardization, stability, and alignment with document-level representations. We introduce LX Topic, a neural topic method that conceptualizes topics as latent linguistic constructs and produces calibrated document-level topic proportions for empirical analysis. LX Topic builds on FASTopic to ensure strong document representativeness and integrates large language model refinement at the topic-word level using alignment and confidence-weighting mechanisms that enhance semantic coherence without distorting document-topic distributions. Evaluations on large-scale Amazon and Yelp review datasets demonstrate that LX Topic achieves the highest overall topic quality relative to leading models while preserving clustering and classification performance. By unifying topic discovery, refinement, and standardized output in a web-based system, LX Topic establishes topic modeling as a reproducible, interpretable, and measurement-oriented instrument for marketing research and practice.

AI.tldr: LX Topic is a neural topic modeling method that conceptualizes topics as latent linguistic constructs, combining FASTopic's document representativeness with LLM-based topic refinement to produce calibrated document-level topic proportions for empirical business research.
AI.motivation: Existing topic modeling approaches function poorly as measurement instruments for business research: probabilistic models produce diffuse topics, neural models are difficult to interpret theoretically, and LLM approaches lack standardization, stability, and document-level alignment.
AI.method: LX Topic builds on FASTopic for strong document representativeness and integrates LLM refinement at the topic-word level using alignment and confidence-weighting mechanisms that enhance semantic coherence without distorting document-topic distributions.
AI.result: Evaluations on large-scale Amazon and Yelp review datasets show LX Topic achieves the highest overall topic quality relative to leading models while preserving clustering and classification performance.
AI.conclusion: LX Topic establishes topic modeling as a reproducible, interpretable, and measurement-oriented instrument for marketing research by unifying topic discovery, refinement, and standardized output in a web-based system.

title: Linguistically Informed Graph Model and Semantic Contrastive Learning for Korean Short Text Classification
comment: 16 pages, 1 Figure, Accepted at DASFAA 2026 (Full Research Paper)
summary: Short text classification (STC) remains a challenging task due to the scarcity of contextual information and labeled data. However, existing approaches have pre-dominantly focused on English because most benchmark datasets for the STC are primarily available in English. Consequently, existing methods seldom incorporate the linguistic and structural characteristics of Korean, such as its agglutinative morphology and flexible word order. To address these limitations, we propose LIGRAM, a hierarchical heterogeneous graph model for Korean short-text classification. The proposed model constructs sub-graphs at the morpheme, part-of-speech, and named-entity levels and hierarchically integrates them to compensate for the limited contextual information in short texts while precisely capturing the grammatical and semantic dependencies inherent in Korean. In addition, we apply Semantics-aware Contrastive Learning (SemCon) to reflect semantic similarity across documents, enabling the model to establish clearer decision boundaries even in short texts where class distinctions are often ambiguous. We evaluate LIGRAM on four Korean short-text datasets, where it consistently outperforms existing baseline models. These outcomes validate that integrating language-specific graph representations with SemCon provides an effective solution for short text classification in agglutinative languages such as Korean.

AI.tldr: LIGRAM is a hierarchical heterogeneous graph model for Korean short-text classification that addresses challenges of limited contextual information and language-specific characteristics through multi-level graph construction and semantics-aware contrastive learning.
AI.motivation: Existing short text classification methods predominantly focus on English and fail to incorporate Korean's linguistic characteristics like agglutinative morphology and flexible word order, creating a need for language-specific approaches.
AI.method: LIGRAM constructs hierarchical heterogeneous graphs at morpheme, part-of-speech, and named-entity levels, then integrates them to capture Korean grammatical and semantic dependencies. It also applies Semantics-aware Contrastive Learning (SemCon) to reflect semantic similarity across documents.
AI.result: LIGRAM consistently outperforms existing baseline models on four Korean short-text datasets, demonstrating superior performance for Korean short-text classification.
AI.conclusion: Integrating language-specific graph representations with SemCon provides an effective solution for short text classification in agglutinative languages like Korean, addressing both contextual limitations and linguistic characteristics.

title: MIND: Unified Inquiry and Diagnosis RL with Criteria Grounded Clinical Supports for Psychiatric Consultation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have advanced medical dialogue systems, yet psychiatric consultation poses substantially higher demands due to subjective ambiguity and comorbidity complexity: an agent must continuously extract psychopathological cues from incomplete and inconsistent patient reports in multi-turn interactions and perform rigorous differential diagnostic reasoning. However, existing methods face two fundamental challenges. First, without criteria-grounded clinical supports, they are prone to unsupported clinical assertions when symptoms are atypical or underspecified. Second, in multi-turn interactions, they struggle to mitigate inquiry drift (off-topic or low-yield questioning) and optimize questioning strategies. To address these challenges, we propose MIND, a unified inquiry--diagnosis reinforcement learning framework for psychiatric consultation. Specifically, we build a Criteria-Grounded Psychiatric Reasoning Bank (PRB) that summarizes dialogue context into clinical retrieval states, retrieves semantically similar reference consultations, and distills reusable criteria-grounded clinical supports to guide criteria-aligned inquiry and reasoning. Building on this foundation, MIND enforces explicit clinical reasoning with rubric-based process rewards to provide fine-grained supervision over intermediate decision steps, and incorporates a value-aware trajectory rectification mechanism to jointly improve information acquisition and diagnostic decision-making across turns. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MIND consistently outperforms strong baselines in diagnostic accuracy, empathetic interaction quality, interpretability, and generalization.

AI.tldr: MIND is a reinforcement learning framework for psychiatric consultation that uses criteria-grounded clinical supports and process rewards to improve diagnostic accuracy and interaction quality in multi-turn dialogues.
AI.motivation: Psychiatric consultation poses higher demands than general medical dialogue due to subjective ambiguity and comorbidity complexity. Existing methods face two challenges: 1) prone to unsupported clinical assertions without criteria-grounded supports, and 2) struggle with inquiry drift and suboptimal questioning strategies in multi-turn interactions.
AI.method: Proposes MIND framework with: 1) Criteria-Grounded Psychiatric Reasoning Bank (PRB) that summarizes dialogue context into clinical retrieval states, retrieves similar reference consultations, and distills reusable criteria-grounded supports; 2) Explicit clinical reasoning with rubric-based process rewards for fine-grained supervision; 3) Value-aware trajectory rectification mechanism to jointly optimize information acquisition and diagnostic decisions across turns.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate MIND consistently outperforms strong baselines in diagnostic accuracy, empathetic interaction quality, interpretability, and generalization.
AI.conclusion: MIND addresses fundamental challenges in psychiatric consultation by integrating criteria-grounded clinical supports with reinforcement learning, enabling more accurate, interpretable, and effective multi-turn diagnostic dialogues.

title: Order Is Not Layout: Order-to-Space Bias in Image Generation
summary: We study a systematic bias in modern image generation models: the mention order of entities in text spuriously determines spatial layout and entity--role binding. We term this phenomenon Order-to-Space Bias (OTS) and show that it arises in both text-to-image and image-to-image generation, often overriding grounded cues and causing incorrect layouts or swapped assignments. To quantify OTS, we introduce OTS-Bench, which isolates order effects with paired prompts differing only in entity order and evaluates models along two dimensions: homogenization and correctness. Experiments show that Order-to-Space Bias (OTS) is widespread in modern image generation models, and provide evidence that it is primarily data-driven and manifests during the early stages of layout formation. Motivated by this insight, we show that both targeted fine-tuning and early-stage intervention strategies can substantially reduce OTS, while preserving generation quality.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "Order-to-Space Bias" (OTS) in image generation models where entity mention order spuriously determines spatial layout and role assignments, introduces OTS-Bench for quantification, shows the bias is data-driven and occurs early in layout formation, and demonstrates mitigation strategies.
AI.motivation: Modern image generation models exhibit systematic biases where the textual order of entities incorrectly influences spatial arrangements and entity-role bindings, overriding grounded cues and causing layout errors. This bias needs systematic study and quantification.
AI.method: Introduces OTS-Bench to isolate order effects using paired prompts differing only in entity order, evaluates models on homogenization and correctness dimensions. Analyzes bias origins through data-driven investigation and early layout formation stages. Proposes mitigation via targeted fine-tuning and early-stage intervention strategies.
AI.result: Order-to-Space Bias is widespread across modern image generation models. Evidence shows it is primarily data-driven and manifests during early layout formation stages. Both targeted fine-tuning and early-stage intervention strategies can substantially reduce OTS while preserving generation quality.
AI.conclusion: The systematic Order-to-Space Bias in image generation models requires attention as it causes incorrect layouts and role assignments. The proposed OTS-Bench enables quantification, and the identified mitigation strategies offer practical solutions to reduce this bias while maintaining generation quality.

title: ErrorLLM: Modeling SQL Errors for Text-to-SQL Refinement
summary: Despite the remarkable performance of large language models (LLMs) in text-to-SQL (SQL generation), correctly producing SQL queries remains challenging during initial generation. The SQL refinement task is subsequently introduced to correct syntactic and semantic errors in generated SQL queries. However, existing paradigms face two major limitations: (i) self-debugging becomes increasingly ineffective as modern LLMs rarely produce explicit execution errors that can trigger debugging signals; (ii) self-correction exhibits low detection precision due to the lack of explicit error modeling grounded in the question and schema, and suffers from severe hallucination that frequently corrupts correct SQLs. In this paper, we propose ErrorLLM, a framework that explicitly models text-to-SQL Errors within a dedicated LLM for text-to-SQL refinement. Specifically, we represent the user question and database schema as structural features, employ static detection to identify execution failures and surface mismatches, and extend ErrorLLM's semantic space with dedicated error tokens that capture categorized implicit semantic error types. Through a well-designed training strategy, we explicitly model these errors with structural representations, enabling the LLM to detect complex implicit errors by predicting dedicated error tokens. Guided by the detected errors, we perform error-guided refinement on the SQL structure by prompting LLMs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ErrorLLM achieves the most significant improvements over backbone initial generation. Further analysis reveals that detection quality directly determines refinement effectiveness, and ErrorLLM addresses both sides by high detection F1 score while maintain refinement effectiveness.

AI.tldr: ErrorLLM is a framework that explicitly models text-to-SQL errors using a dedicated LLM for SQL refinement, addressing limitations of existing self-debugging and self-correction approaches through structural feature representation, static error detection, and dedicated error token modeling.
AI.motivation: Existing SQL refinement paradigms face two major limitations: (1) self-debugging becomes ineffective as modern LLMs rarely produce explicit execution errors that can trigger debugging signals, and (2) self-correction exhibits low detection precision due to lack of explicit error modeling grounded in question and schema, and suffers from severe hallucination that frequently corrupts correct SQLs.
AI.method: ErrorLLM explicitly models text-to-SQL errors within a dedicated LLM by: (1) representing user question and database schema as structural features, (2) employing static detection to identify execution failures and surface mismatches, (3) extending semantic space with dedicated error tokens that capture categorized implicit semantic error types, and (4) using a well-designed training strategy to explicitly model errors with structural representations, enabling detection of complex implicit errors by predicting dedicated error tokens.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that ErrorLLM achieves the most significant improvements over backbone initial generation. Analysis reveals that detection quality directly determines refinement effectiveness, and ErrorLLM addresses both sides by achieving high detection F1 score while maintaining refinement effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: ErrorLLM provides an effective framework for text-to-SQL refinement by explicitly modeling errors through structural representations and dedicated error tokens, overcoming limitations of existing self-debugging and self-correction approaches, with detection quality being a key determinant of refinement success.

title: Confidence-Calibrated Small-Large Language Model Collaboration for Cost-Efficient Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate superior reasoning capabilities compared to small language models (SLMs), but incur substantially higher costs. We propose COllaborative REAsoner (COREA), a system that cascades an SLM with an LLM to achieve a balance between accuracy and cost in complex reasoning tasks. COREA first attempts to answer questions using the SLM, which outputs both an answer and a verbalized confidence score. Questions with confidence below a predefined threshold are deferred to the LLM for more accurate resolution. We introduce a reinforcement learning-based training algorithm that aligns the SLM's confidence through an additional confidence calibration reward. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method jointly improves the SLM's reasoning ability and confidence calibration across diverse datasets and model backbones. Compared to using the LLM alone, COREA reduces cost by 21.5% and 16.8% on out-of-domain math and non-math datasets, respectively, with only an absolute pass@1 drop within 2%.

AI.tldr: COREA is a cost-efficient reasoning system that cascades a small language model (SLM) with a large language model (LLM), using confidence-based deferral and reinforcement learning for confidence calibration to balance accuracy and cost.
AI.motivation: LLMs provide superior reasoning but at high computational cost, while SLMs are cheaper but less accurate. The paper aims to develop a system that achieves LLM-level accuracy with reduced cost by intelligently combining SLM and LLM capabilities.
AI.method: COREA uses a cascaded approach: 1) SLM first attempts to answer questions, outputting both answer and verbalized confidence score; 2) Questions with confidence below a threshold are deferred to LLM; 3) Reinforcement learning trains SLM with confidence calibration reward to improve both reasoning and confidence estimation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show COREA improves SLM's reasoning ability and confidence calibration across diverse datasets and model backbones. Compared to using LLM alone, it reduces cost by 21.5% on out-of-domain math datasets and 16.8% on non-math datasets, with only ≤2% absolute pass@1 drop.
AI.conclusion: COREA effectively balances accuracy and cost in complex reasoning tasks through confidence-based cascading and reinforcement learning-based confidence calibration, demonstrating practical cost savings with minimal accuracy degradation.

title: T2S-Bench & Structure-of-Thought: Benchmarking and Prompting Comprehensive Text-to-Structure Reasoning
comment: Dataset and Code have been released at https://t2s-bench.github.io/T2S-Bench-Page/
summary: Think about how human handles complex reading tasks: marking key points, inferring their relationships, and structuring information to guide understanding and responses. Likewise, can a large language model benefit from text structure to enhance text-processing performance? To explore it, in this work, we first introduce Structure of Thought (SoT), a prompting technique that explicitly guides models to construct intermediate text structures, consistently boosting performance across eight tasks and three model families. Building upon this insight, we present T2S-Bench, the first benchmark designed to evaluate and improve text-to-structure capabilities of models. T2S-Bench includes 1.8K samples across 6 scientific domains and 32 structural types, rigorously constructed to ensure accuracy, fairness, and quality. Evaluation on 45 mainstream models reveals substantial improvement potential: the average accuracy on the multi-hop reasoning task is only 52.1%, and even the most advanced model achieves 58.1% node accuracy in end-to-end extraction. Furthermore, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SoT alone yields an average +5.7% improvement across eight diverse text-processing tasks, and fine-tuning on T2S-Bench further increases this gain to +8.6%. These results highlight the value of explicit text structuring and the complementary contributions of SoT and T2S-Bench. Dataset and eval code have been released at https://t2s-bench.github.io/T2S-Bench-Page/.

AI.tldr: SoT prompting guides LLMs to construct intermediate text structures, boosting performance across 8 tasks and 3 model families. T2S-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating text-to-structure capabilities, revealing substantial improvement potential in current models.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by how humans handle complex reading tasks by marking key points, inferring relationships, and structuring information. The authors explore whether large language models can similarly benefit from explicit text structure to enhance text-processing performance.
AI.method: 1) Introduce Structure of Thought (SoT) prompting technique that explicitly guides models to construct intermediate text structures. 2) Present T2S-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating text-to-structure capabilities, with 1.8K samples across 6 scientific domains and 32 structural types, rigorously constructed for accuracy, fairness, and quality.
AI.result: Evaluation on 45 mainstream models shows substantial improvement potential: average accuracy on multi-hop reasoning is only 52.1%, and even the most advanced model achieves only 58.1% node accuracy in end-to-end extraction. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SoT yields +5.7% average improvement across 8 tasks, and fine-tuning on T2S-Bench increases this to +8.6%.
AI.conclusion: Explicit text structuring significantly enhances LLM performance on complex text-processing tasks. SoT prompting and T2S-Bench provide complementary approaches for improving text-to-structure capabilities, with the benchmark revealing substantial room for improvement in current models.

title: Semantic Bridging Domains: Pseudo-Source as Test-Time Connector
summary: Distribution shifts between training and testing data are a critical bottleneck limiting the practical utility of models, especially in real-world test-time scenarios. To adapt models when the source domain is unknown and the target domain is unlabeled, previous works constructed pseudo-source domains via data generation and translation, then aligned the target domain with them.
